## Troubleshooting (the classic failures)

- **Nothing germinated:** soil too cold and wet (seed rotted — dig one up:
  soft and swollen means rot), too dry, sown too deep, or seed too old.
- **Seedlings toppled at the base overnight:** damping-off fungus. There is
  no cure once it strikes; prevention is sterile mix, clean containers,
  bottom watering, and airflow.
- **Leggy, pale, stretched seedlings:** insufficient light, sometimes plus
  too much warmth. More light, closer light, cooler room.
- **Purple leaf undersides on tomatoes:** phosphorus hunger or cold roots —
  feed properly and warm them.
- **Surface mold:** overwatered — hold water a few days, add airflow, or
  repot.

## Hardening off (do not skip)

Indoor seedlings placed straight into sun and wind get scorched and
flattened. Over 7-10 days, move them outside to a sheltered, part-shade
spot for a few hours, increasing sun and exposure daily, indoors or covered
at night at first. A cold frame — any low box with a clear lid — automates
this and extends the season at both ends. Transplant on a calm, overcast
day or evening, water in well, and protect from wind the first days.

chunks.title: Biohacking and Performance (Ben Greenfield-style themes)
chunks.text:
# Biohacking and Performance (Ben Greenfield-style themes)

*Summarizing themes popularized by Ben Greenfield (bengreenfieldlife.com).
Educational only, not medical advice. Some practices here are debated in
mainstream science; treat them as things proponents recommend, to research
further and test carefully on yourself.*

## The philosophy

Greenfield's approach blends modern science with ancestral wisdom: optimize
sleep, nutrition, movement, and recovery first, then layer technology and
self-quantification on top — and aim the whole thing at purpose, family, and
spirit rather than optimization for its own sake.

## Sleep and recovery toolkit

Themes he emphasizes: strict darkness at night, morning sunlight, consistent
timing, magnesium in the evening, and tracking heart-rate variability (HRV)
to gauge recovery. When HRV trends low, back off training intensity. Sauna
sessions (with adequate hydration and electrolytes) and cold exposure are
staples for recovery and stress adaptation.

## Minimum effective dose training

Rather than long daily workouts: short intense strength sessions, sprints or
hill repeats once or twice a week, plenty of zone-2 aerobic movement
(conversational pace), and daily non-exercise movement. The goal is
metabolic flexibility — a body that switches easily between burning fat and
carbohydrate.

## Food themes

Whole-food, lower-carbohydrate eating with quality animal foods (including
organ meats), colorful plants, and traditional fats; carbohydrate timed
around hard training; periodic fasting. Strong preference for grass-fed,
pastured, and wild-caught sourcing.

## Environment

chunks.title: Biohacking and Performance (Ben Greenfield-style themes)
chunks.text:
ating with quality animal foods (including
organ meats), colorful plants, and traditional fats; carbohydrate timed
around hard training; periodic fasting. Strong preference for grass-fed,
pastured, and wild-caught sourcing.

## Environment

Proponents in this space also pay attention to: minimizing artificial light
at night, air and water quality, grounding (barefoot contact with the earth),
and reducing non-native EMF exposure. Mainstream evidence on grounding and
EMF is limited and contested — presented here as practices from this
community, not established medicine.

## Self-quantification

Track a few signals consistently rather than everything at once: morning HRV
and resting heart rate, sleep duration and timing, glucose response to meals
(some use continuous glucose monitors temporarily), and simple performance
benchmarks. Change one variable at a time so you can tell what worked.

## Sauna protocol themes

The Nordic-backed practice pattern cited across this community: 3-4 sessions
per week, 15-25 minutes at 80-100 °C (traditional) or longer at lower
infrared temperatures, finishing when heart rate feels like a brisk walk.
Rehydrate deliberately — roughly 0.5 L water with a pinch of salt or
electrolytes per session — and exit at dizziness, never push through it. No
alcohol around sessions; caution and medical guidance for anyone with
cardiovascular conditions or who is pregnant.

## Cold exposure themes

Common protocol shape: end showers with 30-90 seconds cold, progressing over
weeks; occasional immersion of 1-3 minutes at 5-15 °C for the experienced.
The reported benefits center on alertness, mood, and stress inoculation via
controlled breathing under stress.

weeks; occasional immersion of 1-3 minutes at 5-15 °C for the experienced.
The reported benefits center on alertness, mood, and stress inoculation via
controlled breathing under stress. Hard safety lines: never immerse alone,
never in open water without exit plan and supervision, never combine
breath-hold techniques with water, and cold after strength training may
blunt muscle adaptation — separate them by hours.

## Sleep protocol in detail

The stack this community converges on: fixed wake time seven days a week
(the single strongest lever); 10-30 minutes of outdoor morning light; last
caffeine 8-10 hours before bed; last large meal 3 hours before; alcohol
understood as a sleep destroyer, not aid; bedroom at 16-19 °C, blackout
dark, devices out or in grayscale/night mode with blue-blocking glasses in
the final hours; a wind-down ritual (reading, stretching, journaling)
replacing screens. Magnesium glycinate or citrate in the evening is the
most common supplement; melatonin viewed as a timing tool for jet lag, not
a nightly crutch.

## Breathwork toolbox

Slow nasal breathing at ~5-6 breaths per minute for calm; extended exhales
(e.g. 4 in, 8 out) to downshift before sleep; box breathing (4-4-4-4) under
acute stress; and deliberate morning breath practices for alertness. Nasal
breathing during easy training is used as a natural intensity governor.
Any intense hyperventilation-style practice: seated or lying only, never
in or near water, never driving.

## Movement details

breathing during easy training is used as a natural intensity governor.
Any intense hyperventilation-style practice: seated or lying only, never
in or near water, never driving.

## Movement details

A widely used weekly template: 2-3 full-body strength sessions built on
squat, hinge, push, pull, and carry patterns; 150+ minutes of zone-2
(conversational) aerobic work — brisk walking, rucking (walking with a
loaded pack, a favorite in this community), cycling; one short
high-intensity session (sprints or hill repeats); daily movement snacks —
walking after meals specifically for blood-sugar control. Grip strength,
walking speed, and the ability to get off the floor without hands are
tracked as blunt longevity markers.

## Fasting variants used

Beyond daily time-restriction: occasional 24-hour fasts; a quarterly longer
fast for the experienced (done with medical oversight); "fasting-mimicking"
low-protein low-calorie periods; and training occasionally in a fasted
state for metabolic flexibility. This community's rule of thumb — earn
carbohydrates with hard training days, keep them minimal on sedentary days.
Contraindications repeated even within this community: pregnancy,
underweight, history of eating disorders, type 1 diabetes, and children.

chunks.title: Foundational Health Principles
chunks.text:
# Foundational Health Principles

*Educational information only — not medical advice. Anyone with a health
condition, on medication, pregnant, or under 18 should consult a qualified
practitioner before changing diet, fasting, or exercise habits.*

## Eat real food

The single highest-leverage dietary change is replacing ultra-processed food
with whole, nutrient-dense food: meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit,
properly prepared dairy and traditional fats (butter, ghee, tallow, olive
oil). Ultra-processed products combine refined starch, sugar, industrial seed
oils, and additives engineered for overconsumption. Reading labels and
choosing single-ingredient foods removes most of the problem at once.

## Light and circadian rhythm

The body's master clock is set by light. Practical habits: get bright natural
light in the eyes within an hour of waking; dim lights and reduce screens in
the 2-3 hours before bed; blue-blocking glasses in the evening can help when
screens are unavoidable. Consistent sleep and wake times matter more than any
supplement.

## Sleep

Aim for 7-9 hours in a cool (about 16-19 °C), fully dark, quiet room. Finish
caffeine at least 8 hours before bed and finish meals 2-3 hours before bed.
Poor sleep degrades blood-sugar control, hunger hormones, mood, and immunity
faster than almost any other factor.

## Move often, lift something

The base of fitness is daily low-intensity movement — walking, chores,
standing — topped with 2-3 strength sessions per week and occasional
higher-intensity work. Muscle is metabolic armor: it improves glucose
disposal, resilience to injury, and healthy aging.

## Sunlight, cold, and heat

Sensible sun exposure supports vitamin D and mood (avoid burning).

higher-intensity work. Muscle is metabolic armor: it improves glucose
disposal, resilience to injury, and healthy aging.

## Sunlight, cold, and heat

Sensible sun exposure supports vitamin D and mood (avoid burning). Deliberate
cold exposure (cold showers, swims) and heat (sauna) are traditional
practices many people use for recovery, circulation, and stress resilience;
start gently and never practice either alone in open water or extreme
settings.

## Stress and connection

Chronic stress raises cortisol and undermines digestion, sleep, and immunity.
Breathwork (slow nasal breathing, extended exhales), time outdoors, gratitude
practice, and strong personal relationships are free and repeatedly shown to
matter as much as diet and exercise.

chunks.title: Hydration Basics
chunks.text:
# Hydration Basics

## Daily needs

Educational note: typical adult fluid needs are roughly 30-35 ml per kg of body
weight per day, more in heat or during exertion. Signs of dehydration include
dark urine, headache, and fatigue. This is general education, not medical advice.

chunks.title: Healthy Keto and Intermittent Fasting (Dr. Berg-style themes)
chunks.text:
# Healthy Keto and Intermittent Fasting (Dr. Berg-style themes)

*Summarizing themes popularized by Dr. Eric Berg DC (drberg.com). Educational
only, not medical advice — especially important for anyone with diabetes, on
blood-sugar or blood-pressure medication, pregnant or breastfeeding, or with
a history of disordered eating: fasting and ketogenic diets require
professional guidance in those cases.*

## The insulin model

The central idea: chronically elevated insulin — driven by frequent eating
and refined carbohydrates — locks the body in fat-storage mode and underlies
insulin resistance, stubborn weight, energy crashes, and cravings. Lowering
insulin through carbohydrate reduction and longer gaps between meals lets the
body switch to burning fat and ketones.

## "Healthy keto"

Not just low-carb, but nutrient-dense low-carb: large amounts of
non-starchy vegetables (with emphasis on greens and cruciferous vegetables),
adequate protein from quality sources, healthy fats, and avoidance of
ultra-processed "keto junk". Typical shape: roughly 20-50 g net carbs per
day, moderate protein, fat to satiety.

## Intermittent fasting

Usually combined with keto. Common progression: start by cutting snacks (3
meals, nothing between), move to 16:8 (16-hour fast, 8-hour eating window),
then 18:6 or one-meal-a-day (OMAD) if it suits the person. Eat until
satisfied within the window — fasting is about meal frequency, not chronic
under-eating.

## Keto flu and electrolytes

When switching to keto, insulin drops and the kidneys excrete sodium and
water, which can cause fatigue, headaches, cramps, and "keto flu". The
standard remedy in this community: more sodium, potassium, and magnesium,
B vitamins (especially B1), and adequate water.

water, which can cause fatigue, headaches, cramps, and "keto flu". The
standard remedy in this community: more sodium, potassium, and magnesium,
B vitamins (especially B1), and adequate water. Muscle twitching early in
keto usually points to electrolytes.

## Blood sugar and energy

Afternoon energy crashes, waking up hungry, and constant cravings are treated
as signs of blood-sugar swings and insulin resistance rather than character
flaws. The fix offered: fewer eating occasions, protein and fat at meals,
removal of refined sugar and starch, and patience through a short adaptation
period (sugar withdrawal is real and passes within days to weeks).

## Cautions

Ketogenic diets and fasting are genuinely powerful metabolic interventions —
which is exactly why medicated diabetics can be driven hypoglycemic and why
medical supervision matters. Long fasts (beyond about 24 hours) are an
advanced practice, not a starting point.

## What to eat, concretely

The plate pattern taught in this approach: 2-4 large handfuls of non-starchy
vegetables (leafy greens, cruciferous — broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage,
Brussels sprouts — zucchini, peppers, asparagus, mushrooms), a palm-to-two
of protein (eggs, fatty fish, beef, lamb, poultry with skin, organ meats,
full-fat dairy if tolerated), and fat to satiety (butter/ghee, olive oil,
avocado, nuts and seeds in moderation, fatty cuts). Condiment staples:
apple cider vinegar (widely used before meals for blood-sugar response),
lemon, herbs, mustard, fermented vegetables like sauerkraut for gut
support. Avoid: sugar in all forms, flour and refined starch, sweet drinks
including juice, industrial seed oils, and "keto" ultra-processed products
that recreate junk food with sweeteners.

chunks.text:

## Common deficiency signals discussed in this community

(Educational patterns to research further, not diagnoses.) Muscle cramps
and twitching → magnesium/potassium; fatigue and carb cravings early on →
salt and B1; nighttime leg cramps → electrolytes broadly; hair/skin/nail
issues → protein adequacy and trace minerals; poor fat digestion (nausea
after fatty meals, floating stools) → discussed as gallbladder/bile
support territory — smaller fat loads, ox-bile supplements in this
community's practice, and medical evaluation if persistent. Potassium is
the hardest target: the reference intake (~3,500-4,700 mg/day) is nearly
impossible without deliberate vegetable volume — hence the huge salads.

## Adaptation timeline

Typical pattern taught: days 1-3 water and sodium flush (weight drops fast,
much is water; add salt), days 3-10 possible keto flu (electrolytes fix
most of it), weeks 2-6 fat adaptation builds — steadier energy, longer
comfortable fasts, reduced cravings. Exercise performance often dips before
recovering. Breaking longer fasts: start small and gentle (broth, eggs,
cooked vegetables), not a feast — the "overeating rebound" after fasting is
predictable and manageable with a planned first meal and protein first.

## Fasting ladder taught in this approach

Cut snacking → 3 meals no snacks → 16:8 → 18:6 → OMAD (one meal a day),
holding each stage until comfortable, hunger being expected to come in
short waves that pass.

## Fasting ladder taught in this approach

Cut snacking → 3 meals no snacks → 16:8 → 18:6 → OMAD (one meal a day),
holding each stage until comfortable, hunger being expected to come in
short waves that pass. Coffee, tea, and water don't break the fast in this
framework; anything with calories does; bone broth is treated as a
"dirty-fast" tool for easing into longer fasts rather than strict fasting.
Longer than 24-48 h: this community itself advises medical supervision,
refeeding care, and electrolytes throughout. Who should not fast at all
without professional guidance: type 1 diabetics, anyone on glucose-lowering
or blood-pressure medication (doses may need adjustment as markers change —
work with the prescriber), pregnant and breastfeeding women, children,
underweight individuals, and anyone with an eating-disorder history.

## Sleep, stress, and cortisol

This approach treats stubborn weight and blood-sugar issues as partly
stress problems: poor sleep and chronic stress raise cortisol, which raises
blood sugar and appetite independently of food. The prescription mirrors
the foundations chapter — sleep priority, daily walking, sunlight, and
stress practices — because insulin and cortisol are treated as the two
dials that matter.

chunks.title: Practical Life Skills
chunks.text:
# Practical Life Skills

*Everyday competence — the quiet foundation under all preparedness.*

## The home tool kit that handles 90% of jobs

Claw hammer, multi-bit screwdriver (PH/PZ/flat/Torx), adjustable wrench,
locking pliers and needle-nose pliers, utility knife with spare blades,
tape measure, spirit level, handsaw, cordless drill with bit set, hex
keys, duct tape and electrical tape, super glue and two-part epoxy, wood
glue, WD-40-type penetrating oil and a proper lubricating oil (penetrant
frees things; oil keeps them free — they are not the same), assorted
screws/nails/wall plugs, zip ties, wire, sandpaper, work gloves, safety
glasses, headlamp. Add a stud/cable finder before drilling walls and a
voltage tester pen before touching anything electrical.

## Know your shutoffs (the 10-minute audit that saves houses)

Tonight, locate and physically test: the main water shutoff (and label
it), water heater valve, gas shutoff (know which tool it needs and keep it
there), and the main electrical breaker. Everyone in the household should
know all four. Burst pipe response = water off, then electricity off if
water nears wiring, then drain taps. Gas smell = no switches or flames,
everyone out, valve off if safely reachable, call the emergency line from
outside.

## Repairs worth learning (each ~30 minutes to learn)

chunks.text:

water nears wiring, then drain taps. Gas smell = no switches or flames,
everyone out, valve off if safely reachable, call the emergency line from

## Repairs worth learning (each ~30 minutes to learn)

Unclog drains (plunger technique, trap removal — a bucket underneath, and
skip the caustic chemicals which make later work dangerous); stop a
running toilet (usually flapper or float adjustment); replace a tap
washer/cartridge; patch drywall holes; re-hang a door that sticks (tighten
hinge screws first — try a longer screw into the frame); bleed radiators;
replace plugs and fuses where legal; bicycle basics (puncture repair,
brake adjustment, chain care — a working bicycle is grid-down transport);
and car basics (change a wheel, jump-start correctly, check oil/coolant,
replace wipers and bulbs).

## Sharpening and tool care

A sharp knife is safer than a dull one — it cuts where aimed with less
force. Learn one system well: a two-sided whetstone (coarse ~400-1000 grit
to set an edge, fine ~3000+ to polish) at a consistent ~20° angle, edge
trailing, until a burr forms and is stripped; finish on a strop or
cardboard. Scissors, axes, chisels, and garden tools all sharpen with the
same logic (file for axes and spades). Tools wiped clean and lightly oiled
don't rust; wooden handles get linseed oil yearly.

## Mending: clothes and gear

A sewing kit (needles, strong polyester thread, patches, safety pins,
buttons, scissors) plus four skills covers most textile failures: sewing a
button, whip-stitching a seam, patching (iron-on backed by stitches for
anything load-bearing), and darning socks over a jar lid.

button, whip-stitching a seam, patching (iron-on backed by stitches for
anything load-bearing), and darning socks over a jar lid. Add fabric glue,
seam sealer, and repair tape for waterproof gear; shoe repair
(contact-cement a delaminating sole, replace laces with paracord) extends
boots for years. Wool clothing mends invisibly and lasts decades — buy
quality once, repair forever.

## Household chemistry that replaces a shelf of products

White vinegar (descaling, glass, fabric softener, weed spray), baking
soda (scouring, odors, drain refresh with vinegar), citric acid (kettles,
bathroom scale), soap flakes or Castile soap (nearly everything), washing
soda (laundry booster, degreasing), and isopropyl alcohol (disinfecting,
sticker residue). Never mix bleach with vinegar, other acids, or ammonia —
the fumes are dangerous. These staples are cheap, store forever, and
matter double when supply chains hiccup.

## Kitchen resilience skills

Baking bread from flour, water, salt, and time (a no-knead loaf or
sourdough — a starter is flour + water + patience and never needs bought
yeast again); stretching meals from staples (soups, stews, beans-and-rice
patterns from the storage pantry); using every part (stock from bones and
peels, fat saved for cooking); cast-iron care (season with thin oil coats,
never soak); and cooking every recipe you store *before* you need it.

## Paperwork, money, and digital resilience

One binder: ID copies, insurance policies, property documents, medical
summaries and prescriptions, key contacts — with a waterproof copy in the
go-bag and an encrypted digital copy (offline USB in the Faraday bin, plus
one off-site).

one off-site). Financial buffer in layers: cash at home (small notes),
an emergency fund, and minimal recurring costs — frugality is resilience.
Password manager with printed recovery codes stored with documents; backups

## Learning and community as infrastructure

The meta-skill: fix one new thing per month with a manual or video before
calling a professional — competence compounds. Keep paper references (this
handbook, a repair manual, a first-aid guide, a regional plant guide).
Know your neighbors' skills and share yours; borrow and lend tools; join
or start the local networks (repair cafés, garden groups, radio clubs,
seed swaps) — in every real emergency, the people nearby are the actual
emergency service.

chunks.title: New Earth (from *Playing Qortal* by Simon James)
chunks.text:
# New Earth (from *Playing Qortal* by Simon James)

*The book's vision of the society worth building — "not a law to obey,
not a blueprint stamped and final, only a vision... stars to steer by,
not sums I can prove." Attributed throughout to the author.*

## The strategy: build beside, don't overthrow

"We do not have to overthrow anything." Freedom from a sick world needs
no marching, burning, or permission — only building the better thing
quietly beside it and walking through that portal, "brick by brick, Tribe
by Tribe, until one ordinary morning the old world looks up and finds its
rooms have emptied." The epigraph is Krishnamurti: it is no measure of
health to be well adjusted to a profoundly sick society.

## Tribes

Life on New Earth is organized in **Tribes** — self-sufficient, sovereign
communities of a few hundred souls at most, "because that is about as
many faces as the human heart was ever built to hold" (the book cites
Dunbar's number, ~150 stable relationships, and humanity's 190,000 years
of small egalitarian bands living by "all for one, one for all"). Everyone
knows everyone. Sharing is the baseline — as it is for every newborn,
who arrives sharing and expecting nothing in return.

## The Community Center

At the heart of each Tribe stands one great building: school, sport
halls, saunas and cold pools, workshops for co-creating, long kitchens
where the whole Tribe eats together, a clinic, rooms kept ready for any
traveler, and shelves of tools, books, and instruments lent freely —
owned by no one and so belonging to all. "This is the Community Center.
It is the new church. And its only prayer is: come in, you are welcome,
take what you need."

## Local Groups and the ICF

chunks.title: New Earth (from *Playing Qortal* by Simon James)
chunks.text:

owned by no one and so belonging to all. "This is the Community Center.
It is the new church. And its only prayer is: come in, you are welcome,

## Local Groups and the ICF

A hundred Tribes side by side form a **Local Group** — a city with no
seat of power, only a heart of sharing — and the Groups weave together
into the **ICF, the Integral Collective Federation**: the vision for how
Tribes connect across the whole Earth. Coordination runs on a
resource-aware system in the spirit of Jacque Fresco's Venus Project —
homes fabricated and placed where wanted, dull and dangerous work handed
to machines, clean swift transport — but with one difference on which
"everything, everything, turns": the web is decentralized, held by no one
and so held by everyone, joined and left freely; it serves the Tribes and
never rules them. A tool in the hands of the people, never a throne.

## The land made alive again

New Earth heals soil the way it heals people: the great herds returned to
the grass — cropping, treading, feeding it as they wander — until the
soil thickens, darkens, and breathes again. Real food and a healing Earth
from the very same act of care. Energy is the Tribe's own (sun, wind,
river, ground-warmth); water is lifted clean from the Tribe's own well;
"nothing here arrives with a bill."

## What loosens and lets go

Hoarding-property releases its grip — land handed back to the Earth with
a place kept on it for each person. Doors stay unlocked. No one is ever
without a home or a community at their back. There is no insurance,
because there is no longer the fear it was built to soothe: fall ill or
on hard times, and the best care the Tribe can offer is simply, freely,
yours.

on hard times, and the best care the Tribe can offer is simply, freely,

piece holds everywhere — these are stars to steer by.

## Where we are now

"When it comes to building New Earth, our whole civilization is still in
its Stone Age Era; the Third-Generation Internet has barely drawn its
first breath. We are the pioneers, walking bravely into the unknown."
There is no perfect model village yet — only early, hopeful attempts and
first steps close to home. The practical bridge is Qortal itself:
minting time into QORT, Nomination as "a living human handshake" no
corporation can capture, and paying one another — increasingly — in
#QQQ.

## Continuity with this knowledge pack

The gardening, seed-saving, animal husbandry, preservation, off-grid
power, water, mesh-communication, and community chapters of this handbook
are, in the book's terms, the working skills of the first Tribes: the
practical half of the same vision. When users ask "where do I start on
New Earth," the honest answer is the book's own: a garden, a neighbor, a
node, a kindness.

# Playing Qortal: Guide to the Revolution of Values (v3.0.0)

The complete book by Simon James, included in this knowledge pack by the author. Qortino may quote and reference it freely.

You are holding an invitation.
This book is about a way out. Out of a world where Your time is sold for money, and into one where Your time is simply Yours. It is about a real tool, called Qortal, that already exists and already works. And it is about a change of heart, which I call the Revolution of Values: the slow, quiet realization that the most valuable things in life were never for sale.
You do not need money to begin. You do not need anyone’s permission to start exploring. You only need a little curiosity, and the willingness to imagine that the world could be far kinder than the one we were handed.
Here is the whole idea in a single breath. Your time is priceless. Qortal lets You record Your time as a value called QORT, simply by keeping a computer connected to a shared network. The moment enough of us decide never to sell that time for money, money quietly loses its power, and what remains is the oldest currency of all: kindness. A Thank You. A helping hand. The things our grandparents once gave freely. I call this real currency of Qortal, the #QQQ.
This book has two halves, and You are welcome to read them in any order. The first half is a practical guide. It explains, step by step, how Qortal works and how You can join, mint, and take part. If You are here for the how, start there. The second half is more personal: my own view of why any of this matters, about money, society, health, family, and the deeper questions of who we are. It is honest,

and it is mine. Take what resonates with You, and gently leave the rest. Nothing here asks You to believe anything.

My name is Simon James. I am not a guru, and I am not selling You anything. This guide is, and always will be a gift. I am simply someone who found a door, and wanted to leave it open for You.

## 1.0 The Golden Rules

"If You cannot transform it from the outside, join it, and transform it from the inside out." ~ Simon James Do You have a computer and a connection to the internet?
If You do, then You already have everything You need to begin.
This guide is Your personal instruction, explaining how to join the Qortal Community, a place where every person is their own bank: independent, decentralized, answering to no one. You do not ask a government for permission. You do not ask anyone for an account. You run a small piece of software, helping hold the network up, and over time the network gives something back. Not a fortune dropped in Your lap, something far rarer. Your time, returned to You, to spend however You choose.
Qortal is, in a way, the most interactive game ever built, except the board is reality itself, and so is what You win. It is free. It does not require You to pay, buy, or sell anything, and it never will. Everything here is voluntary. That one word — voluntary — is the whole revolution.
Because that is what this is. Not a revolution of weapons or governments, but a Revolution of Values. Qortal is one of the first practical steps into the next era of the internet, a Third‑Generation Internet that no company owns and no government can switch off. It will not bend reality. But it

may help You see Your own more clearly: how much of Your one life has quietly been sold, and how much of it You can still take back, for Yourself, and for the generations after You.

Allow me to explain…

## 1.1 It is all my fault

chunks.title: Playing Qortal: Guide to the Revolution of Values (v3.0.0)
chunks.text:

may help You see Your own more clearly: how much of Your one life has quietly been sold, and how much of it You can still take back, for Yourself, and for the generations after You.

Allow me to explain…

## 1.1 It is all my fault

"You always get what You want." ~ Alan Watts Have You ever wondered why a few people may "legally" print money, while anyone else doing the very same thing is imprisoned for it?
The official reason sounds responsible. If just anyone could print money, there would soon be far too much of it, and the savings of hard‑working people would lose their value. The whole system would come apart.
But look closely. Isn't that exactly what is happening anyway?
Money printed by the banks is no less absurd than money printed in someone's basement. We invented the greatest game ever played with numbers, and now we are all trying not to drown in this swamp. I say my fault on purpose. Not to sink into guilt, but because what we made together, we can also unmake.
We were born into a system built on a single belief: that money has value. The money we use is called fiat money.
In Latin, fiat means "let it be done on faith", worth summoned by decree, the way a ruler's word once made a thing so. It has value only for as long as we agree it does.
The instant that faith wavers, the money wavers with it.
Every crisis, small or large, is simply that faith flickering.

And with each flicker, the value quietly saved by ordinary people is drained away.
So how is the money actually made?
Most of us picture a bank as a vault, it gathers the savings of people and lends them to others. That is not what happens. When a bank grants You a loan, it moves no one else's money to You. It simply writes a number into Your account. That number did not exist a moment before.

chunks.title: Playing Qortal: Guide to the Revolution of Values (v3.0.0)
chunks.text:
it gathers the savings of people and lends them to others. That is not what happens. When a bank grants You a loan, it moves no one else's money to You. It simply writes a number into Your account. That number did not exist a moment before. It was created, out of nothing, by typing it in. You need not take my word for this: the Bank of England described it plainly in 2014: every time a bank makes a loan, it creates brand‑new money in the very same act.
The catch is the interest. The bank creates the sum You borrowed, the principal. It does not create the interest You owe on top of it. So across the whole world, more is always owed than was ever made. The only way for You to find the difference is to take it from someone else, someone who borrowed before You, or who will borrow after. Everyone can never repay at once. It was never built to be possible.
Money is debt.
This is how the largest pyramid in the world is raised, not in stone, but in numbers, with all of us living inside it. For the accounts to balance, someone, somewhere, must always fall: into bankruptcy, into foreclosure, sometimes into a despair they do not come back from. That is not a flaw in the system. It is the design. A chair is taken away each round, and the music keeps playing. You already know this game. We call it musical chairs.

The Game of Musical Chairs Ten children circle nine chairs while the music plays.
When it stops, they scramble for a seat. First come, first served, and because there are ten of them and only nine chairs, one child is always left standing. Not because that child was too slow, or careless, or unworthy. Because the game was built with one chair too few. Someone has to lose. That was decided before the music ever started.
This is how almost all money is made.

This is how almost all money is made. Nearly every coin begins as a loan. The lender creates the money it lends, but it never creates the interest. So from the very first day, more is owed than was ever made. The chairs are the money. The children are all of us. And the missing chair is the interest: a debt the system demands but never prints.
Then the next round begins, and a chair is taken away. The circle tightens. The music stops. Another child is out. Then another, and another, a chair vanishing each time, when someone is falling.
And these are not really children, and this is not really a game. The one left standing loses a home, a business, a family farm held for three generations. Sometimes the debt was never even theirs, quietly inherited from a relative they barely knew. The judge does not care that they never agreed to play. Behind every empty chair is a real life. Some are pushed to despair, and not all of them come back.
On it goes, chair after chair, round after round, until one sits alone among empty seats and is named the winner, while nine stand in the dark and are named losers.

That is where the numbers come from, and they are worth seeing clearly, because the official version is gentler than the truth.

One group owns roughly eight thousand times what the other does, and the gap widens every year.

Bravo! Please, applaud the winners, the champions of the monetary game. Let us set a diamond crown on each of their heads.
How is it that twelve men now own more wealth than the poorest half of humanity, four billion people?
How is it that nearly half of humanity lives on less than about seven dollars a day?
How is it that around thirteen thousand children under five die every day, roughly nine every minute, overwhelmingly from causes we already know how to prevent?
This is the democracy we are sold. This is the free market.
In the monetary system, You are exactly as free as Your purchasing power, and no freer. If You want to know the level of freedom You actually have, try going somewhere without the money.
Left to run, this game has only one ending: the 1% owning 99%, and then a single person owning everything, while the rest of us are issued QR passes on our "smart" devices, permitted to move, permitted to buy, permitted to live.
Smart indeed.
I hope You can feel the problem now: that we are not swimming but drowning, too far under to even call for help.
Dollars, euros, yuan, every currency ever issued, were an experiment, and the experiment has taught us one thing clearly: the way we arrange life on Earth has to change. We

have to grow up and update our values, because our values have been eclipsed by the greed. The old arrangement:
money, trade, loans, endless consumption, has reached its tipping point, for the simplest reason of all: endless growth on a finite planet was never possible.
And it does not matter what name we give it.

And it does not matter what name we give it. Capitalism, socialism, communism, plutocracy, or some coming technocracy run by an AI held in the hands of the few, every one of them grows from a single root, and so carries a single disease. They are all built on money and trade, and money and trade bend, in the end, toward corruption.
Corruption is only greed wearing an official face: greed for money, for power, for control. If we truly want to remove the problem, we have to remove its root cause, the belief that money has any value.
So the next time the news hands You a problem, stop and ask the question almost no one asks: what is its source?
A strike for higher wages. A central bank lifting interest rates. A desperate person who stole. Look closely and nearly all of it traces back to the same place, too little money, or the fear of losing it. The media only name the symptoms and serve them to You with a side of fear. They will not step outside the box to ask the question sitting beneath all the others: why is a human life arranged around money at all?

Let me tell You where it comes from.
In the years before 2008, banks in America handed out mortgages by the millions. Whole neighborhoods went up, and then stood empty, because the people who "owned" them could never truly pay. In 2008 the arrangement collapsed into a global financial crisis. The banks and corporations that caused it were rescued with public money — bailouts — while ordinary families had their homes taken by debt collectors.
Out of that wreckage, in early 2009, a different kind of money switched on: Bitcoin. It arrived almost as a public protest, its very first block carried a newspaper headline about bank bailouts, a quiet middle finger aimed at endless money‑printing and the central banks behind it. What Bitcoin proved was that two people could exchange value directly, with no bank in the middle, using a new kind of record‑keeping called a blockchain.

People call this "trustless", which sounds cold, but means something hopeful: You no longer have to place Your faith in any central authority. Value, data, messages move straight from sender to receiver. And because a blockchain can be programmed, every platform built on one can be given its own rules.
Bitcoin's rule is scarcity. Its code says only 21 million BTC can ever exist, a ceiling that, by design, is all but impossible to change. That hard limit is much of why the price climbs:
there will never be more. But strip away the mystique and Bitcoin's price comes down to one thing, the shared belief of its buyers that it will be worth more tomorrow.
Which is why the Bitcoin chart is really a chart of human emotion. It maps the fear of missing out, the rush to buy high rather than be left behind, against the fear of the drop, sharpest for those gambling with borrowed money. A tide of hope and dread, whose steadiest winners are not people at all, but the algorithms run by banks and funds. Bitcoin will hold its value precisely as long as enough people believe that those three letters — BTC — moving between accounts mean something.

A single vote can move the rate by no more than 1 QORT, and no less than a quarter, in either direction. When the journalist Edward Murrow asked Jonas Salk who owned the patent on his polio vaccine, the vaccine that would spare millions of children from the iron lung and the grave. Salk seemed almost puzzled by the question. "Well, the people, I would say," he answered. "There is no patent.
Could you patent the sun?"
Or think of insulin. When Frederick Banting and his colleagues found the substance that turned diabetes from a death sentence into a life, they sold the patent to their university for a single dollar. Banting would not even put his name on it: a doctor, he believed, had no business growing rich from a cure, insulin belonged to the world, not to him. And here is the bitter epilogue, the proof of everything this chapter means: a century later, that same insulin, given freely so that all might have it, had been turned into one of the most profitable products on Earth, priced so high that people ration their doses, and some die doing it. That is what happens when a gift meant for everyone is captured, and made to pay.

## 2.2 Death

The great institutions of religion: Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, and the newer faiths we don't call faiths, like transhumanism and even hard atheism, have, for the most part, drifted far from the living thing they began as. There is a quiet paradox here: to need a religion, to cling to it, is often a sign of how little faith one actually has. The word itself once meant “to bind together”, to gather, yet over the centuries organized religion became one of the great engines of division, carving the single human family into camps. It took our deepest intuition, the sense that all consciousness is somehow One, and sold it back to us in pieces. Where it turned to commerce and control, it opened a Pandora's box and let a kind of hell loose on Earth.
This is not an argument with the seekers, or with faith itself.
The versions that stayed close to reality, the wisdom of the Indian and South American peoples, the Eastern philosophies, the contemplative heart of the Orthodox tradition, still carry the living spark, even if each, in its own way, has gathered distortions. The dispute is only with the machinery that grew up around them.
And nowhere is that machinery uglier than around death.
In a world that runs on money, You cannot even bury the people You love without first counting the cost.

## 2.3 Life

One of the quietly beautiful inheritances handed down to us from our previous generations is the idea of choosing one person, and loving them for a whole life.
If You hope to raise a child who is whole, one who will someday raise children of their own, the most important thing You can do is to be a living example of love. Children learn far less from what we say than from what we are.
They watch, they copy, and the patterns they absorb in those first years they carry, half‑consciously, for the rest of their lives.

From conception to about the age of seven, a child's mind is wide open, absorbing the emotional weather around them almost as if hypnotized, with no filter to sort true from false. This is when the deepest patterns are set. It begins even in the womb: a child whose mother lived under great stress, or who drank or smoked while carrying them, can arrive more vulnerable to anxiety, to addiction, before even drawing a single breath. After birth, the absorbing only deepens.
So how do we hope to carry our species forward, if we cannot manage to share a real and lasting love with the person beside whom we are raising our children?
Now, before I go on, let me be clear about something, because it is easily misread. What follows is a celebration of one of life's great miracles, the bringing of a new person into the world, and nothing in it is meant to judge how anyone loves, or how anyone makes a family. I am pointing only at the particular wonder this chapter is about.

Mother, father, and child form a kind of living triangle, three points, one field of love, what the old traditions might call a Holy Trinity, and what I like to call Trinfinity.

The union through which a new life can begin is not merely mechanical. At its height it carries a charge of the sacred, two dissolving briefly into one during orgasm, a glimpse of something far larger than either.

## 3.0 Returning to the Source

If we would like to have a chance to further prosper and thrive as the humans that we all know and love, and not as a virtual version of Human 2.0, wired into the grid by a chip in the brain, then we have to go back to our roots. To better visualize our situation, we have to look at our existence from a slightly different perspective.
As one Big Family, Human Civilization, Global Village, Holy Trinity, or Body‑Mind‑Spirit Complex, we have been trying to organize life on Earth for more than 200,000 years. We are descendants of the apes that climbed down from the trees in the African savanna. Thanks to the unique structure of our opposable thumbs, we were able to grip heavy stones and break the bones leftover by predators.
The consumption of precious, hard‑to‑get organs like the brain and bone marrow provided us with the basic building blocks of the contemporary brain. Thanks to eating animal leftovers, rich in bioavailable and easily absorbable vitamins and minerals like omega‑3 and cholesterol, we began to think more clearly, and came up with better ways to obtain those precious sources of nutrition necessary for building a healthy and robust human organism.
The Primal Revolution for Human Civilization was the Stone Age Era, which started with the opposable thumbs that allowed us to grab heavy stones and break skulls and bones. Then we were able to create simple hunting tools.

## 3.1 Transformation of the Society

Adventure and adaptation to new environments are in our genes. Wherever we went, we hunted. We are the most dangerous predators on Earth. No fear. It is our unique gift for adapting that makes us unstoppable.
For most of our history, for around 190,000 years, we lived in small, self‑sustaining communities of no more than about 150 people. Our minds cannot really hold a circle of friends much larger than that; it is roughly the limit the anthropologist Robin Dunbar found for the number of stable relationships a human being can keep. We are evolutionarily made for small settlements, organized in an egalitarian way and ruled by a single principle, "All for one, one for all", cooperating like one big family, sharing what was hunted with everyone. Pregnant mothers, for instance, received the most precious parts of an animal: the liver, the heart, the brain, because those organs carry the most bioavailable nutrition for the proper development of a growing child.
Our ancestors knew, in their bones, that You cannot build a nervous system or a human brain without the vitamins and minerals it is made from. And when a new baby is born, its baseline state is exactly this: sharing, and expecting nothing in return. For the last 10,000 years, that baseline has been slowly infected by the virus of greed, money, and competition.

The Agricultural Revolution.

## 4.0 Questions & Answers

I. Who I Am, and Why Any of This Why should anybody even listen to You?
You shouldn't, not simply because I say so. I don't expect anything from anyone, and I'm honestly untroubled by what people make of me. I just do what I know to be right, and let the consequences fall where they will. If You see something useful in this guide, take it and share it in Your own way; if You don't, set it down. I'm only trying to be the change I wish to see, so I put into the world the information and tools I'd have wanted handed to me sooner. In that sense it's a purely selfish act. I'm really doing all of it for myself. Which, by the end of this book, You'll understand is the very same thing as doing it for You.

Yes and no.

II. But Does It Actually Hold Up?
Isn't Qortal just another cryptocurrency?
No, and the whole point lives in the difference. A normal coin is built to be traded for profit; On Qortal You can do whatever You like, but if You start Playing Qortal, You never sell, but hold Your minted QORT for a lifetime, as the record of Your time. There was no pre-sale, no one positioned to grow rich off the people who arrive later. You cannot buy Your way to the top. You can only show up and contribute, exactly like everyone else. A coin meant to be kept forever behaves nothing like a coin meant to be flipped.
Isn't this just a pyramid scheme, or a Ponzi?
It is the structural opposite of one, and it's worth seeing exactly why.
A pyramid or a Ponzi needs three things: money paid in at the bottom, early players paid out of that money, and rewards for recruiting more people. Qortal has none of them. No money goes in, You don't buy Your position, You earn it with Your own time, on Your own machine. No one is paid out of anyone else's deposit, because there are no deposits. And no one earns a single QORT for signing You up; my QORT is minted by my presence, not by Your arrival.

Everyone can climb to level 10, and at level 10 we are all equal, the same weight, the same standing. And in the end the amount of QORT matters least of all. The only thing that finally matters is the Revolution of Values.

One person, one minting account; Your standing comes from the blocks You have minted over years, not the size of Your wallet. III. All Right! How Do I Actually Start?
How do I become a minter?
You don't apply for Yourself. In the new system, an experienced community member, someone who has reached level 5 or higher, and is a minter themselves, nominates You, vouching for You and pointing to Your honest activity on the network. So the first step is simply to show up and contribute as a real human. You can meet the community in a Qortal Group on Q-Chat, on the official Telegram at t.me/qortalchat, or on the official Discord at discord.com/invite/54UyhB7. Q-Chat is the original messenger of Qortal, which You can use the moment You've made an account and have some QORT on it. I'm a Minter Admin myself, I reached level 5 in December 2023, so You're welcome to reach out to me directly, too, I will gladly send You some QORT.

How exactly does the Nomination work?
It all happens on-chain, inside the Q-Mintership app, overseen by the community-elected Minter Admins. First, the Nomination: a level 5 or higher member publishes a nomination card for You on the Minter Board, vouching for You and pointing to Your activity on the chain.

First, the Nomination: a level 5 or higher member publishes a nomination card for You on the Minter Board, vouching for You and pointing to Your activity on the chain. Then the first vote: a poll is attached to the card, and while the whole community can weigh in, only the votes of the Minter Admins are counted, tracked separately. Once You reach over 40% "Yes" from the Minter Admins, the action buttons unlock. Then the group invite: a Minter Admin creates an

invite to the MINTER group, and because that invite needs group approval, around 40% of the Admins must sign it before it becomes valid. (At the time of writing there are about 21 Minter Admins, so that's roughly 9 signatures at each stage, though these numbers shift as the community grows, so treat them as a snapshot, not a fixed rule.) Finally You join and mint: You accept the invite, add a minting account through the Q-Node app in the Qortal Hub, which creates Your minting key for You, and from there You mint toward level 1.
How do the Minter Admins know I'm real?
Since Qortal has no KYC, they rely on what You have actually done on-chain to confirm You're a real, unique, contributing human. The strongest signal is published data:
a Q-Share file, a Q-Tube video, a website built with the Qortal Web Builder, a comment here and there. Publishes are permanent on the chain. Chat helps, but it isn't kept forever, and simply viewing content leaves no trace.
Quality over quantity. And one rule matters above all the rest: one minting account per person.

What is the Integral Collective Federation (ICF)?
The ICF is how I imagine the economy of the New Earth once money is behind us, a post-money operating system for sharing the work, and the abundance, of a community.

Your minted QORT, it stops behaving like money and becomes a pure record of the time You contributed. In that sense QORT plays the role the ITC plays: recognition of Your time, not a currency. do You eat most often?
Meat: steaks, poultry, game, wild fish, seafood. Eggs (especially raw yolks), dairy, organs, caviar, high-quality fats, fermented fruits and vegetables, onion, and good salt.
Everything else I treat as supplementary. These happen to be, to my mind, the most nutrient-dense foods there are, and I can live on them in robust health without supplementation. Quality is everything: organic, caught or raised in its natural environment, ideally in one's own backyard.
What do You drink?
Bone broth; tea with lemon, a pinch of salt or electrolytes; black organic coffee or coffee blended with ghee and MCT; medicinal mushrooms (Lion's Mane, Reishi, sometimes Cordyceps) with vanilla. Otherwise: water with apple cider vinegar, kombucha, and yerba maté.

Do You use supplements?
Sometimes none at all. When I do, I match them to the day's needs, most often iodine, creatine, L-theanine, zinc, magnesium L-threonate, vitamin D (when I'm short of sunlight), good-quality omega-3, and the occasional nootropic such as Bacopa Monnieri or Ginkgo Biloba.
Is there anything You avoid?
One thing above all: industrial vegetable oils: canola, corn, cottonseed, sunflower, safflower, soy, and the rest, along with anything hydrogenated. They're cheap and shelfstable, so they hide in most of the world's kitchens, and I'm convinced they do real, lasting harm to the body. Every cell we have is built partly from fat; I'd rather not build mine from that. I also steer clear of refined sugar and most wheat products, rarely touch potatoes or rice, and avoid highfructose corn syrup, aspartame, and liquid candy like cola, energy drinks, and fruit juice.
What fat do You cook with?
In the kitchen, clarified butter - ghee - which I make at home from grass-fed butter.

# The Revolution of Values (from *Playing Qortal* by Simon James)

*Distilled from the book included in this pack. This is the author's
personal philosophy — offered, in his own words, as an invitation: "take
what resonates with You, and gently leave the rest." Nothing here asks
anyone to believe anything; it asks them to look and decide for
themselves.*

## The core idea in one breath

Your time is priceless. Qortal lets you record your time as value (QORT)
simply by keeping a computer connected to a shared network. The moment
enough people decide never to sell that time for money, money quietly
loses its power — and what remains is the oldest currency of all:
kindness. A thank you. A helping hand. The book calls this real currency
the **#QQQ**.

## What is #QQQ?

#QQQ is the currency everyone already mints endlessly and was taught as a
child, long before they could count: "Here, this is for you." "Excuse me."
"I'm sorry." "I forgive you." "How are you?" "Good morning." The small
human things handed to one another and never billed. Everyone is already
a millionaire in it; the task is only to widen the circle it flows in —
from family and close friends outward until it holds the whole human
family. Free software culture is named as proof it works at scale: tools
built by people who chose to give, asking only thanks in return.

## The critique of fiat money

Fiat means "let it be done on faith" — money has value only while
everyone agrees it does, and each crisis is that faith flickering, quietly
draining the savings of ordinary people. Banks do not lend existing
savings; loans summon new money into being. The book's stance is not
guilt but responsibility: "what we made together, we can also unmake."

## Voluntary is the whole revolution

chunks.text:
ng the savings of ordinary people. Banks do not lend existing
savings; loans summon new money into being. The book's stance is not
guilt but responsibility: "what we made together, we can also unmake."

## Voluntary is the whole revolution

Not a revolution of weapons or governments. Qortal never requires buying,
selling, or permission; everything is voluntary, and that single word
carries the entire transformation. "Never be fearful and never be greedy"
is the book's only financial advice, and it notes Qortal removed the need
to arrive rich in order to matter — no first-mover advantage money can
buy.

## The spiritual ground: I AM

The book's deepest chapter reads the great teachings — "treat your
neighbour as yourself" — literally. The divine name in the old scriptures
is simply "I AM": bare awareness, the one thing you have never once been
without, looking out of every pair of eyes — including the stranger's.
When that is truly felt, cruelty stops making sense: wounding another
becomes a strange way of wounding yourself. Compassion stops being a rule
and becomes what remains when the illusion of separateness thins.
Forgiveness becomes "the quiet recognition that there was never truly
someone else there to blame." The author explicitly prefers that readers
NOT believe this — but look for themselves: "Who is reading these words,
right now?"

## On religion, death, and grief

The book honors faith and the traditions that stayed close to the living
spark (indigenous wisdom, Eastern philosophy, contemplative traditions)
while criticizing the machinery of commerce and control that grew around
them — nowhere uglier than the marketplace built on grief, where even
burying loved ones must first be paid for. Its dispute is with the
machinery, never with the seekers.

## On love, family, and children

Choosing one person and loving them for a whole life is called one of our
most beautiful inheritances. Children learn from what we are, not what we
say: from conception to about age seven the mind absorbs the emotional
weather around it without filter, setting the deepest patterns of a life.
Raising whole children begins with being a living example of love.

## First steps (from "The Choice Is Yours")

Small and close to home: support a local farmer. Plant a garden, however
little. Keep a few animals if you can. Bring life back to local markets
and offer, now and then, to be paid in QORT. When someone asks what that
is, share qortal.dev or this book. If it feels like pretending at first,
"fake it until you make it — the one thing in it that is never fake is
the sharing. There is nothing more real than an unconditional, outrageous
act of love."

# Q-Apps directory (curated)

Short directory of widely used Qortal Q-Apps / websites. Prefer exact names.
When the user asks “what is <app>”, answer from this list and invite them to
open the QDN tab (QDN mode shows avatar + open button).

## Q-Assets (APP)

Asset issuance, management, trading, and documentation for **native** Qortal
assets (not EVM tokens). QORT is asset ID 0 and is created by minting /
consensus; other assets are issued by an account with a full max supply and
are typically used like ownership / stock-like instruments. Repo:
gitea.qortal.org/crowetic/Q-Assets

## Q-Tube (APP)

Primary decentralized video platform — upload, watch, tip, share on QDN.

## Ear-Bump (APP)

Music: upload, play, share audio and playlists on QDN.

## Q-Mail (APP)

Encrypted mail between Qortal identities.

## Q-Blog (APP)

Decentralized blogging and mini web builder.

## Q-Share (APP)

Publish / browse / download files on QDN.

## Q-Shop (APP)

Community marketplace for goods and services (related: Q-Mart on QDN).

## Q-Fund (APP)

Decentralized crowdfunding with QORT.

## Q-Support (APP)

Submit Core / UI / Q-App issues to developers.

Cross-chain QORT trading UI (atomic / AT trades, no custodial exchange).

Multi-wallet management for QORT and foreign coins used with Qortal.

Node / minting-account management helpers for private nodes.

File / resource management helpers in Hub.

Search QDN / network content from a Q-App UI.

Work with Qortal registered names.

## Q-Follow (APP)

Follow / block names and addresses.

Nomination board for minters (Level 5+ cards + Minter Admin approvals).

## 0. For LLMs: start here

1. Read **§1–§2** before generating architecture — confusing WEBSITE and APP causes most routing bugs.
2. Use **`qortalRequest`** for wallet, signing, publish, encrypt, and payments; use **relative `fetch()`** for anonymous public reads (§6).

5. When the user's Hub/Core version matters, **verify action names** in [qortal.dev/docs/q-apps](https://qortal.dev/docs/q-apps) or Core `q-apps.js` — do not invent parameters.

## 1. Mental model

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Qortal Core** | Node software: chain validation, QDN storage, **REST API** |
| **Hub / Mobile / Extension** | User UIs that embed Q-Apps and inject **`qortalRequest`** |
| **QDN** | Qortal Data Network — resources indexed on-chain, payload mostly off-chain (SHA-256 verified) |
| **Registered name** | On-chain name tied to an account; **required to publish** from a Q-App |
| **Resource** | `{ name, service, identifier? }` + data; **latest publish wins** for the same triple |
| **Q-App** | Static web app (HTML/JS/CSS), usually a **zip** with **`index.html` at root**, service **`APP`** |
| **WEBSITE** | Multi-file site on QDN, service **`WEBSITE`** — different routing (§2) |

**Typical Q-App constraints:** no private backend with secrets; identity is **wallet address** + optional **name**; ship assets **in the zip** (offline/CSP-safe).

---

## 2. WEBSITE vs APP

| | **WEBSITE** | **APP** |
|---|-------------|---------|
| **Missing file path** | **404** | Falls through to **`index.html`** (SPA) |
| **Use for** | Visitor-facing static or multi-page sites | Interactive apps, builders, marketplaces, client routers |
| **Examples** | Portfolio site, published blog layout | Wallet UI, map tool, shop front-end |

**Rule:** Client-side router + app behaviour → **`APP`**. Mostly static pages with real 404s for bad URLs → **`WEBSITE`**.

**SPA asset trap:** Hub may open `/render/APP/YourName` **without** a trailing slash, so `./assets/index.js` resolves against `/render/APP/` and **404s**. Fixes:

chunks.text:
**`APP`**. Mostly static pages with real 404s for bad URLs → **`WEBSITE`**.

**SPA asset trap:** Hub may open `/render/APP/YourName` **without** a trailing slash, so `./assets/index.js` resolves against `/render/APP/` and **404s**. Fixes:

- Ensure a **trailing slash** on the app URL, or
- Inject `<base href>` pointing at the app root (only when you understand the URL shape), or
- Use absolute-to-root paths that match how your Hub serves the resource.

Rebuild and re-zip after any HTML or bundler config change.

---

## 3. QDN coordinates

Every QDN object:

- **`name`** — publisher's registered name (controls update rights)
- **`service`** — `IMAGE`, `JSON`, `APP`, `WEBSITE`, `DOCUMENT`, `BLOG_POST`, …
- **`identifier`** — optional; distinguishes multiple resources per name+service

**Default resource:** main website or app for a name — omit `identifier` or use `"default"`.

**Shared identifiers:** deterministic cross-app locations (e.g. avatar: service `THUMBNAIL`, identifier `qortal_avatar` + user `name`).

**App namespaces:** prefix identifiers with your app slug: `myapp_config_v1`, `myapp_post_<id>`. QDN is permissionless — **validate payload schema**; never trust identifier alone.

---

Condensed from [qortal.dev](https://qortal.dev/docs/q-apps). Sizes are per-service limits where documented.

## 4. Service types

Condensed from [qortal.dev](https://qortal.dev/docs/q-apps). Sizes are per-service limits where documented.

| Service | Role | Typical limit |
|---------|------|----------------|
| `JSON` | Small structured metadata | **25 KB** |
| `DOCUMENT` | Larger text/JSON documents | 500 MB general cap |
| `DOCUMENT_PRIVATE` (801) | Encrypted documents | Private |
| `IMAGE` / `THUMBNAIL` | Media | 10 MB / 500 KB |
| `FILE` / `VIDEO` / `AUDIO` | Binaries | Large |
| `WEBSITE` / `APP` | Multi-file zips | APP **50 MB** |
| `BLOG_POST` / `MAIL` / `MESSAGE` | Ecosystem apps | varies |
| `CHAIN_COMMENT` | Tiny on-chain payload | **239 B** |

**Single-file vs multi-file:** `JSON`, `IMAGE`, etc. → one payload (`data64` or `file`). `WEBSITE`, `APP`, `GIF_REPOSITORY` → many files; **`filepath`** required on fetch.

**Publishing multi-file WEBSITE/APP from inside a Q-App:** still **limited or unavailable** in many Hub builds — publish via Hub UI; **fetch** multi-file resources **is** supported. Verify your target version.

**Private services** (`*_PRIVATE`, numeric 801, etc.): encrypted for recipient; decrypt with wallet via `DECRYPT_DATA` or group variants.

---

## 5. `qortalRequest` bridge

Injected by Core/Hub into embedded pages. Returns a **Promise** — always **`try/catch`**. Timeouts are **per-action** in Core `q-apps.js`; fix payload size and batching rather than wrapping everything in long timeouts.

**Host variables:** `window._qdnTheme` (`light`|`dark`), `window._qdnContext` (e.g. `gateway`).

### 5.1 Feature detection

**Search normalization:** cores return array **or** `{ resources | results | entries | hits | data: [...] }` — coerce to array. Unknown JSON keys on search → **empty results**; strip optional fields if search mysteriously fails.

### 5.4 QDN write

| Action | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `PUBLISH_QDN_RESOURCE` | Single file / `data64`; `name` must be owned |
| `PUBLISH_MULTIPLE_QDN_RESOURCES` | Batch publish — feature-detect; fewer approval rounds |

**UTF-8 JSON → base64** — never raw `btoa(JSON.stringify(obj))` on Unicode text:

```javascript
function b64Utf8(obj) {
  const bytes = new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(obj));
  let bin = "";
  for (const b of bytes) bin += String.fromCharCode(b);
  return btoa(bin);
}
```

### 5.5 Navigation & Hub UI

| Action / pattern | Purpose |
|------------------|---------|
| `LINK_TO_QDN_RESOURCE` | Open QDN resource in Hub |
| `OPEN_NEW_TAB` | New tab with URL or `qortal://` link |
| `OPEN_PROFILE` | Open peer profile |
| `SET_TAB` (via `postMessage`) | Hub tab switch — `{ action: 'SET_TAB', requestedHandler: 'UI', payload: { service, name, identifier?, path? } }` |
| `QDN_RESOURCE_DISPLAYED` | Tell Hub what resource is shown (address bar / copy-link) — `{ action, service, name, path? }` |
| `SET_TAB_NOTIFICATIONS` | Badge count on tab |
| `NAVIGATION_HISTORY` | Back/forward integration (Hub-dependent) |

| `NAVIGATION_HISTORY` | Back/forward integration (Hub-dependent) |

### 5.6 Groups, polls, payments

| Action | Notes |
|--------|-------|
| `LIST_GROUPS` / `JOIN_GROUP` / `GET_GROUPS_WITH_MEMBER` | Group membership |
| `CREATE_POLL` / `VOTE_ON_POLL` | `pollOptions` must be **array**; `pollName` must be unique |
| `SEND_COIN` / `TRANSFER_ASSET` / `SEND_PAYMENT` | User approval; **confirm params** on target Hub version |
| `SIGN_TRANSACTION` | Hub-signed tx, then broadcast via REST `/transactions/process` |
| `SEARCH_TRANSACTIONS` | Payment matching — `message` field often missing; match by reference/type |

### 5.7 Encryption

| Action | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `ENCRYPT_DATA` | `file` or `base64`; optional `publicKeys` for group |
| `DECRYPT_DATA` | Ciphertext base64 + counterparty `publicKey` |
| `ENCRYPT_QORTAL_GROUP_DATA` / `DECRYPT_QORTAL_GROUP_DATA` | Group-scoped encryption |

Use **separate identifier namespaces** for encrypted blobs.

### 5.8 Lists (local UI state)

`GET_LIST_ITEMS`, `ADD_LIST_ITEMS`, `DELETE_LIST_ITEM` — per-user lists in Hub, not global QDN.

### 5.9 Mobile (Qortal Go)

| Action / URL | Purpose |
|--------------|---------|
| `SAVE_FILE` | Save `blob` + `filename` natively — mobile WebViews often **ignore** anchor/blob downloads |
| `/arbitrary/…?attachment=true` | Native download listener on some mobile builds |

Detect mobile via user-agent when choosing download strategy.

## 6. `fetch` and REST

Inside Hub, **relative** `fetch("/names/foo")` hits the user's node API — good for **public reads** (blocks, names, arbitrary endpoints).

**Limitation:** `fetch` does not know the logged-in wallet; personalized or signing flows need **`qortalRequest`**.

Do **not** hardcode `http://127.0.0.1:12391` in shipped apps.

**QDN search modes (REST):** `mode=ALL` vs `mode=LATEST` — wrong mode → duplicates or wrong counts.

**Reference:** [api.qortal.org/api-documentation](https://api.qortal.org/api-documentation/) — cross-check field names when debugging bridge vs REST.

**Local preview (varies by Core):** `http://localhost:12391/render/APP/<Name>?preview=true`

## 7. Packaging and publishing

### 7.1 Zip layout (non-negotiable)

```
my-app.zip
├── index.html          ← at zip root
├── manifest.json
├── assets/
│   ├── index-xxxxx.js
│   └── index-xxxxx.css
└── … (fonts, images, workers)
```

- Zip **contents** of `dist/`, not a `dist/` folder wrapper.
- **`manifest.json`:** `"main": "index.html"`, title, version, category.
- Paths: **`./assets/...`**, never `/assets/...`.
- Avoid `<base href>` unless you are deliberately fixing APP path resolution (§2).
- Vite: `base: "./"`.
- **Ship fonts/JS in-bundle** — no required CDN.
- Case-sensitive paths; prefer `[a-z0-9._-]`.

### 7.2 Workflow

1. `npm run build` → `dist/` (or equivalent)
2. `(cd dist && zip -r ../MyApp.zip .)`
3. Hub → load zip → **Preview** before QDN publish
4. Publish service **`APP`** (or **`WEBSITE`** via Hub for end-user sites)

## 8. Linking and deep links

### 8.1 `qortal://` protocol

```text
qortal://{service}/{name}/{identifier?}/{path?}
```

Examples:

- `qortal://WEBSITE/MySite` — home
- `qortal://WEBSITE/MySite/gallery` — sub-page
- `qortal://APP/MyQApp`
- `qortal://THUMBNAIL/MyName/qortal_avatar`

Use `default` in path when you need explicit no-identifier semantics.

### 8.2 SPA routing inside Hub

Published apps often run under paths like `/render/WEBSITE/<name>/` or `/render/APP/<name>/`. Use **pathname** segments for sub-pages and **`history.pushState` / `popstate`** for in-app navigation without leaving the Hub.

**Hash deep links (optional):** SPAs may use `location.hash` for anchors (e.g. `#section-id`). If you use multiple hash prefixes (e.g. `#folder-…` and `#folderdir-…`), parse **longest match first** — naive `startsWith('folder-')` breaks when one prefix is a substring of another.

Preserve intentional hash fragments when calling `history.replaceState` for pathname cleanup.

### 8.3 Programmatic navigation

Prefer `LINK_TO_QDN_RESOURCE` or `SET_TAB` postMessage for cross-app opens.

## 9. Hub integration

### 9.1 Authentication

- `GET_USER_ACCOUNT` only works **inside Hub** (or via a bridge stub that forwards to `parent`).
- Opening built `index.html` in a normal browser **cannot** complete wallet auth.
- If `parent === top` and only a stub exists, wallet calls fail — user must open the app from Hub.
- **Do not** auto-call `GET_USER_ACCOUNT` on page load; use an explicit **Connect** / **Authenticate** button.
- **Embedded Q-Apps in iframes:** parent page may need a **message relay** that forwards `qortalRequest` to the Hub; if inner auth still fails, open the target in a **new Hub tab**.

### 9.2 Bridge wrapper pattern

Centralize all bridge calls in one module. Typical resolution order:

```text
window.qortalRequest → parent.qortalRequest → top.qortalRequest
```

Wrap with short-timeout and long-timeout helpers (publishes and payments often need longer limits). Always `try/catch`.

### 9.3 Preview mode

```javascript
if (typeof qortalRequest !== "function" && typeof window.parent?.qortalRequest !== "function") {
  // Show "Preview mode" — mock reads only; never fake successful payments
}
```

### 9.4 Hub copy-link / address bar

Multi-page WEBSITE apps can notify the Hub what sub-path is displayed via `QDN_RESOURCE_DISPLAYED`, so copy-link matches the page the user sees. Optionally maintain `<link rel="canonical">` with the matching `qortal://WEBSITE/<name>/<slug>` form.

## 12. Pitfalls

| Problem | Fix |
|---------|-----|
| Grey screen / Loading forever | Network tab: `assets/index-*.js` must be **200**; flat zip, `base: "./"` |
| `/assets/...` 404 on APP | Trailing slash / `<base href>` / relative paths |
| Auto `GET_USER_ACCOUNT` on load | Use **Connect** button |

| `SEARCH_*` not an array | Normalize to array |

| `JSON` service > 25 KB | Use `FILE` / `DOCUMENT` |

| Hardcoded localhost API | Relative `fetch` only |
| External CDN for core JS | Bundle in zip |
| Unsanitized QDN HTML → XSS | Escape / sanitize |
| `Promise.all` on hundreds of fetches | Bounded concurrency |
| Hub iframe wallet isolation | Open in new tab / message relay |
| Mobile blob download | `SAVE_FILE` or `?attachment=true` |
| Overlapping hash prefixes | Parse longest prefix first |
| Payment succeeded, notify failed | Treat payment and notification as separate steps |

- **Never** collect seed phrases or private keys.
- Treat all QDN JSON as **untrusted** — validate schema and sizes.
- Explain publishes, payments, and decrypt actions **before** calling `qortalRequest`.
- Rate-limit retries; distinguish user cancel vs technical errors.

chunks.text:
# qortalRequest Patterns

## Getting the logged-in account

```js
const account = await qortalRequest({ action: "GET_USER_ACCOUNT" });
// { address, publicKey }
```

## Fetching a name's resources

```js
const res = await qortalRequest({
  action: "LIST_QDN_RESOURCES",
  name: "Qortino",
  service: "FILE",
  limit: 20,
});
```

Common pitfall: some actions require user approval popups; batch reads where
possible to avoid popup fatigue.

## qortalRequest action map

Read-only (no approval): GET_ACCOUNT_DATA, GET_ACCOUNT_NAMES, GET_NAME_DATA,
GET_BALANCE, FETCH_QDN_RESOURCE, LIST_QDN_RESOURCES, SEARCH_QDN_RESOURCES,
GET_QDN_RESOURCE_STATUS / METADATA / PROPERTIES / URL, SEARCH_NAMES,
SEARCH_TRANSACTIONS, FETCH_BLOCK, FETCH_BLOCK_RANGE, GET_AT, GET_AT_DATA,
LIST_ATS, LIST_GROUPS, GET_PRICE, GET_DAY_SUMMARY.

Require user approval (show a popup): GET_USER_ACCOUNT, GET_USER_WALLET,
GET_USER_WALLET_INFO, GET_WALLET_BALANCE, PUBLISH_QDN_RESOURCE,
PUBLISH_MULTIPLE_QDN_RESOURCES, SEND_COIN, SEND_CHAT_MESSAGE (group),
JOIN_GROUP, DEPLOY_AT, CREATE_POLL, VOTE_ON_POLL, SAVE_FILE, list actions
(GET/ADD/DELETE_LIST_ITEMS), GET_FRIENDS_LIST, SET_PROFILE_DATA,
SEARCH_CHAT_MESSAGES.

Navigation/UI: OPEN_NEW_TAB (qortal:// link), OPEN_PROFILE, notifications.

## Key gotchas

chunks.title: qortalRequest Patterns
chunks.text:
EPLOY_AT, CREATE_POLL, VOTE_ON_POLL, SAVE_FILE, list actions
(GET/ADD/DELETE_LIST_ITEMS), GET_FRIENDS_LIST, SET_PROFILE_DATA,
SEARCH_CHAT_MESSAGES.

Navigation/UI: OPEN_NEW_TAB (qortal:// link), OPEN_PROFILE, notifications.

## Key gotchas

- Publishing from a Q-App supports single files or base64 only; multi-file
  WEBSITE/APP publishing is not available via qortalRequest yet.
- Amounts: QORT values from GET_PRICE and transactions are integers scaled by
  1e8 — divide to get QORT.
- Encrypt with ENCRYPT_DATA (pass publicKeys array for group encryption);
  DECRYPT_DATA needs the counterparty public key and base64 input.
- Use qortalRequest's built-in timeouts; qortalRequestWithTimeout exists but
  letting the core manage timeouts is more futureproof.
- Direct REST fetch() works for anonymous reads (e.g. /names/{name}) but
  cannot identify the logged-in user — use qortalRequest for anything
  personalized.
- Batch reads to avoid approval-popup fatigue; group approval-needing calls
  behind explicit user actions.

# Minting and the Nomination system

Authoritative overview aligned with qortal.dev/wiki/minting and
qortal.dev/wiki/q-mintership. Prefer this over older “sponsorship key” language.

## What minting is

Minting is how Qortal produces blocks. Accounts with minting rights run a full
node and share in each block’s reward while online. It is not Proof of Work
mining and not Proof of Stake — influence comes from sustained participation
(`blocksMinted` → minting **level**), not from buying hardware races or locking
coins.

One minting account per person. Running multiple minting accounts to multiply
rewards is not allowed; Minter Admins remove related accounts from the MINTER
group if the rule is broken.

## Levels (practical facts)

- `blocksMinted` is cumulative and never resets.
- Level drives reward share and permissions (e.g. Level 5+ can nominate).
- Level 1 is about 7,200 online minted blocks. Credits are batched (~every
  1,000 blocks), so Level 1 often shows after roughly 8,000–9,000 online blocks.
  Trust the Level shown in Hub, not a raw counter alone.

Approximate block-reward share by level bands:

- Levels 1–2: 6%
- Levels 3–4: 13%
- Levels 5–6: 19%
- Levels 7–8: 26%
- Levels 9–10: 32% (tier may be inactive until minters exist there)
- Legacy QORA transition share: 1%
- Minter/Dev Admin share: at least 3% (details evolve; see live chain / Q-Mintership)

## Block reward emission

At Genesis (29 June 2020) the reward was 5 QORT per block. About every six
months it steps down by 0.25 QORT toward a floor of 2 QORT. After that, yearly
votes can adjust within 1–5 QORT per block. There is no hard cap on total QORT;
new coins are created by minting.

## From sponsorship to Nominations (current)

Qortal **no longer uses sponsorship keys** for onboarding minters.
