## From sponsorship to Nominations (current)

Qortal **no longer uses sponsorship keys** for onboarding minters.

Current path = **Nominations** inside the **Q-Mintership** Q-App, approved by
community-elected **Minter Admins** on-chain:

1. A **Level 5+** minter publishes a **nomination card** for you (you cannot
   nominate yourself).
2. A poll opens; community and admin votes are tracked separately.
3. At roughly **40% Minter Admin “yes”**, admin action buttons unlock.
4. An admin creates a **MINTER group invite**; ~40% of admins must sign via
   group approval (~9 of ~21 admins at typical counts — the exact number changes).
5. You **JOIN_GROUP**, then add a minting account in **Q-Node** and keep a
   synced full node online.

What helps a nomination: registered name, real QDN publishes, helpful community
presence, and a nominator who knows your work. Viewing content alone is weak
evidence; durable QDN publishes are strongest.

## Guides to open on QDN

- **Welcome to Qortal** (APP) — onboarding / orientation for newcomers.
- **Q-Minter** (WEBSITE, “Q-Minter Guide”) — detailed minting guide.
- **Q-Mintership** (APP) — live nomination board and admin flow.

When the user is in QDN mode, recommend opening these as QDN tabs.

chunks.title: QDN Basics
chunks.text:
# QDN Basics

## What QDN is

QDN (Qortal Data Network) is Qortal's decentralized data layer. Every piece of
published data is a *resource* identified by three things: a registered **name**,
a **service** type (e.g. WEBSITE, APP, DOCUMENT, FILE), and an optional
**identifier** string. Data is stored and served by nodes that follow the name.

## Publishing a resource

To publish, an account must own a registered name. Publishing costs a fee in
QORT proportional to data size. Common pitfalls:

- Publishing without a registered name fails — register the name first.
- Identifiers are case-sensitive; keep a consistent naming scheme.
- Large files should be chunked or published as FILE service, not DOCUMENT.

### Example

Publish a JSON document from a Q-App:

```js
await qortalRequest({
  action: "PUBLISH_QDN_RESOURCE",
  name: "Qortino",
  service: "DOCUMENT",
  identifier: "qortino_agent_manifest",
  data64: btoa(JSON.stringify(manifest)),
});
```

## Fetching a resource

Q-Apps fetch with `FETCH_QDN_RESOURCE`, specifying name, service, and
identifier. If the resource is not yet locally available the node downloads it
from peers following that name.

## Service types

Every QDN resource declares a service that sets validation rules and size
limits. Common public services: WEBSITE and APP (multi-file, APP max 50 MB),
FILE and FILES, IMAGE (10 MB), THUMBNAIL (500 KB), VIDEO, AUDIO, DOCUMENT,
JSON (25 KB), BLOG and BLOG_COMMENT, LIST, CODE, GAME, NFT, MAIL (1 MB),
MESSAGE, COMMENT, and CHAIN_COMMENT (239 bytes, fully on-chain). Private
variants (e.g. MAIL_PRIVATE, IMAGE_PRIVATE) store data encrypted so only the
recipient's private key can decrypt it.

BLOG_COMMENT, LIST, CODE, GAME, NFT, MAIL (1 MB),
MESSAGE, COMMENT, and CHAIN_COMMENT (239 bytes, fully on-chain). Private
variants (e.g. MAIL_PRIVATE, IMAGE_PRIVATE) store data encrypted so only the
recipient's private key can decrypt it. Resources under 240 bytes can live
fully on-chain; larger payloads are stored off-chain and verified by an
on-chain SHA-256 hash.

## Default resources and shared identifiers

A resource published without an identifier is the "default" for that
name+service — a user's main website is the default WEBSITE for their name.
Apps can use the keyword "default" to address it explicitly. Shared
identifiers create deterministic locations across names: every avatar is
published as service THUMBNAIL with identifier "qortal_avatar", so any app can
fetch any user's avatar knowing only their name.

## App data conventions

Apps should prefix their identifiers with the app name (e.g. "myapp_" +
random suffix) and later search with SEARCH_QDN_RESOURCES using the prefix
option. QDN is permissionless, so an app must validate the format of anything
it fetches rather than trust that its own app published it.

## Updating

Publishing again with the same name + service + identifier overwrites the
resource. Only the current owner of the name can update. If a name is sold,
update rights move with it.

chunks.title: Qortal Overview
chunks.text:
# Qortal Overview

## What Qortal is

Qortal is a fully decentralized platform combining a blockchain, a data network
(QDN), a communication layer (Q-Chat), and an application layer (Q-Apps). Its
goal is user sovereignty: identity, data, apps, and value exchange all run on
infrastructure operated by the community, with no central servers. The native
coin is QORT.

## Accounts and names

A Qortal account is a keypair derived from a seedphrase; the address starts
with "Q". To publish data or build a public identity, an account registers a
**name** on-chain. Names are unique, tradeable, and are the anchor for
everything published on QDN. Losing a seedphrase means losing the account —
there is no recovery service, so back it up offline.

## Minting and levels

Qortal replaces mining with **minting**: approved accounts that stay online
with a full node help produce blocks and earn QORT. Accounts progress through
levels (1–10) from `blocksMinted`. Higher levels earn a larger share of each
block reward. New minters join via the **Nomination** system in Q-Mintership
(a Level 5+ nominator + Minter Admin on-chain approval) — not the old
sponsorship-key model. See `minting-nominations.md` for the full flow.

## Groups

On-chain groups provide shared membership, group chat, and group-managed
permissions. Groups can be open or closed (invite/approval based), and
group-encrypted data on QDN is readable only by members.

## The Trade Portal

Qortal includes built-in cross-chain trading. QORT can be traded directly for
coins such as LTC, BTC, DOGE, RVN, DGB, and ARRR using AT (Automated
Transaction) smart contracts — no exchange or custodian involved. Prices are
set by open offers from other users, not an order-matching company.

## Fees and philosophy

## Fees and philosophy

Transactions and QDN publishes cost small QORT fees proportional to data size.
The project's philosophy emphasizes long-term infrastructure independence:
anyone can run a node, host data for names they follow, and use the system
without permission.

chunks.title: Running a Qortal Node and Self-Hosting Your Data
chunks.text:
# Running a Qortal Node and Self-Hosting Your Data

## Why run a node

A node is full participation: it validates the chain, serves QDN data for
names you follow, lets you mint (earn QORT for securing the network), and
keeps your access to Qortal independent of anyone else's infrastructure —
including gateways. In a censored or degraded-internet scenario, locally
synced chain data and QDN content remain usable, and nodes can sync from
any reachable peer.

## Practical requirements

Qortal Core is Java-based and runs on Linux, Windows, macOS, and modest
hardware — a Raspberry Pi 4/5 class machine with 4+ GB RAM and an SSD is a
popular dedicated node. Storage grows with the chain plus whatever QDN
content the node follows/hosts; budget tens of GB and room to grow. An
uninterruptible power supply pairs naturally with minting, since minting
rewards consistent uptime.

## Data hosting model

QDN storage is follow-based: nodes host data published by names they
follow. This means data persistence is social — content stays alive
because people who value it follow its publisher. For your own resilience:
run a node that follows your own name (your published apps and documents
are then always locally held), and encourage community members to follow
names whose content matters to them. Popular content naturally gains
redundancy across many nodes.

## Ports and connectivity

Qortal peers over its own P2P port and serves a local API/UI. Port
forwarding improves peer connectivity but isn't strictly required to use
the network. The local UI and API (used by Q-Apps in the Hub) run against
your own node — which is the trust model working as intended: your node,
your rules, no third-party API dependency.

## Node hygiene

chunks.text:

the network. The local UI and API (used by Q-Apps in the Hub) run against
your own node — which is the trust model working as intended: your node,
your rules, no third-party API dependency.

## Node hygiene

Keep Core updated (updates ship through the network's auto-update
mechanism), back up the account seedphrase offline (the node holds no
custody — accounts are keys, not server records), monitor disk space, and
if minting, verify the minting key is active and blocks-minted is
increasing. A node that has been offline simply resyncs from peers — the
chain is the backup.

chunks.title: Bushcraft and Field Skills
chunks.text:
# Bushcraft and Field Skills

*Educational overview of traditional outdoor skills. Practice in safe,
legal settings before you ever need them. Not a substitute for hands-on
training or professional rescue.*

## The 5 C's of survivability

A widely taught bushcraft framework (popularized by Dave Canterbury) for what
to carry because it is hardest to reproduce in the field:

1. **Cutting tool** — a fixed-blade knife of decent carbon steel; the single
   most important item.
2. **Combustion** — ferro rod plus lighter, and prepared tinder.
3. **Cover** — tarp or emergency blanket, wool layer, rain protection.
4. **Container** — a single-wall metal bottle or pot you can boil in.
5. **Cordage** — paracord or bankline for shelter, repairs, and traps where
   legal.

Extensions add cotton bandana, candle, compass, cargo tape, canvas needle.

## Rule of threes

Rough survival priorities: about 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without
shelter in harsh exposure, 3 days without water, 3 weeks without food. In
cold, wet climates like the North Atlantic, shelter and fire outrank
everything else — hypothermia kills far faster than hunger.

## Fire

Reliable fire is preparation, not sparks: collect tinder (birch bark, fatwood
shavings, dry inner bark), then pencil-thin twigs, then finger- and
wrist-thick fuel, before striking anything. Build on dry ground or a platform
of sticks, protect from wind, and feed gradually. Carry two ignition sources
minimum; a ferro rod works wet and cold when lighters fail.

## Shelter

Site selection first: out of wind, off low ground where cold air and water
collect, away from dead standing trees. The fastest effective shelter is a
tarp in an A-frame or lean-to with insulation underneath you — ground
conduction steals more heat than air.

chunks.title: Bushcraft and Field Skills
chunks.text:
rst: out of wind, off low ground where cold air and water
collect, away from dead standing trees. The fastest effective shelter is a
tarp in an A-frame or lean-to with insulation underneath you — ground
conduction steals more heat than air. Snow and debris shelters work but cost
sweat; avoid soaking your clothing while building.

## Water in the field

Prefer flowing water; collect upstream of activity. Boiling is the most
reliable treatment. Filters handle bacteria and protozoa; chemical treatment
or boiling covers viruses. In winter, melt snow with a little liquid water in
the pot to avoid scorching, and never eat snow directly in cold conditions —
it lowers core temperature.

## Navigation and signaling

Tell someone your route and return time before heading out. Carry a compass
and paper map even with GPS. If lost: stop, stay warm, make yourself visible.
Three of anything (whistle blasts, fires, flashes) is a distress signal.
A whistle carries farther than a voice for far less energy.

## Field first-aid basics

The priorities are stopping severe bleeding (direct pressure first),
protecting airway and breathing, preventing hypothermia in any casualty, and
getting professional help. Carry and know your kit: pressure bandage, gauze,
tape, gloves, blister care, any personal medication. Educational note only —
take a certified first-aid course; hands-on practice is what works under
stress.

## The next-fire mentality

tape, gloves, blister care, any personal medication. Educational note only —
take a certified first-aid course; hands-on practice is what works under

## The next-fire mentality

A discipline taught in bushcraft schools: never consume your last means of
making fire, and prepare the next fire while you still have this one.
Practically: gather and dry tomorrow's tinder beside tonight's fire, keep
char cloth or charred punk wood from each fire in a tin (it catches even
weak sparks), maintain a dedicated dry tinder pouch on your body, and treat
the lighter as the convenience and the ferro rod as the reserve — not the
other way around.

## Winter fire specifics

Cold multiplies every fire mistake. Clear snow to ground or build a raft of
green logs so the fire doesn't melt itself into a pit; harvest standing dead
wood (anything on the ground is soaked); split wood to reach dry cores —
outer surfaces lie; process 3-4x more fuel than feels necessary before
lighting, because leaving a struggling fire to gather more is how winter
fires die. Feather sticks (knife-carved curls on a dry stick) and fatwood
(resin-saturated pine) light when everything else is wet. Warm the ferro rod
and your striking hand first — cold, clumsy hands are the real obstacle.

## Wool: the survival fabric

Wool insulates even when wet (synthetics do too; down and cotton do not),
resists ember burns near fires, dampens odor over multi-day wear, and a
single sturdy wool blanket serves as coat (belted), sleeping system,
stretcher, shelter door, cargo sack, and windbreak. The traditional kit of
wool blanket + oilskin tarp still outperforms much modern gear around open
fire, where sparks destroy nylon.

## Cordage crafts

stretcher, shelter door, cargo sack, and windbreak. The traditional kit of
wool blanket + oilskin tarp still outperforms much modern gear around open
fire, where sparks destroy nylon.

## Cordage crafts

Beyond paracord: tarred bank line (small, strong, knot-friendly) handles
most camp jobs at a fraction of the weight. Learn five knots deeply rather
than twenty poorly: bowline (fixed loop), taut-line hitch (adjustable
tension), trucker's hitch (mechanical advantage), clove hitch (quick
attach), and square lashing (structures). A toggle — a simple carved
stick — turns a loop into a quick-release connector for hanging pots,
tensioning shelter lines, and dragging loads.

## Food from the land (know the law first)

Fishing is the most calorie-positive wild food skill for beginners: a hand
reel, hooks, and line weigh nothing and work while you do other tasks.
Passive methods (multiple baited lines, fish traps, snares for small game)
beat active hunting on energy budget, but are regulated or illegal outside
genuine emergencies in most countries — learn the mechanics, respect the
law, and practice catch-and-release or use them only where permitted. Wild
plants: the safe-learning path is a handful of unmistakable local species
learned from an expert, harvested away from roads and sprayed areas —
never experiment with unknowns. Wild mushrooms deserve their own hard
rule: assume any mushroom is unsafe to eat until an expert confirms the
exact species — there is no shortcut test.

## Primitive navigation

## Primitive navigation

Without a compass: the sun rises roughly east and sets roughly west
(seasonally skewed at high latitudes); a stick's shadow tip marked at two
times gives an east-west line; the North Star (find it via the Big Dipper's
pointer stars) sits due north at your latitude's angle above the horizon.
Pace counting with ranger beads (about 65 double-paces per 100 m for many
adults — calibrate your own) tracks distance in poor visibility. Always
back-bearing: look behind you regularly so the return route is a memory,
not a guess.

chunks.title: Food Storage and Off-Grid Cooking
chunks.text:
# Food Storage and Off-Grid Cooking

*Educational preparedness information.*

## The three-layer pantry

1. **Working pantry (2-4 weeks):** more of what you already eat. Rotate by
   first-in-first-out; write purchase dates on lids with a marker.
2. **Extended storage (3-12 months):** shelf-stable staples — white rice,
   oats, pasta, beans, lentils, canned meat and fish, canned vegetables and
   tomatoes, flour, salt, sugar, honey, cooking oils, coffee/tea, spices.
   Canned food is typically safe well past best-before dates if cans are
   intact, not bulging, rusted through, or leaking; quality declines before
   safety does. Never taste-test a suspect can — botulism is odorless.
3. **Deep storage (years-decades):** dry staples packed for the long haul —
   see below.

## Packing dry goods for decades

The proven method: dry goods sealed in Mylar bags with oxygen absorbers,
inside food-grade buckets with lids. Oxygen removal stops insects (including
eggs already in the grain) and oxidation. White rice, wheat berries, beans,
oats, pasta, sugar, and salt stored this way last 20-30 years. Rules of
thumb:

- 300-500 cc of oxygen absorber per 4 L of packed dry goods; err high.
- Do not pack anything above ~10% moisture (no brown rice, nuts, or oily
  goods long-term — the fats go rancid regardless; brown rice lasts ~6-12
  months).
- Squeeze out air, heat-seal the Mylar with a clothes iron on a straight
  edge, label contents and date. A properly sealed bag pulls tight and
  "bricks" within a day or two as the absorber works.
- Sharp dry pasta punctures thin bags and vacuum seals over time — pad the
  ends, double-bag, or choose short shapes.

chunks.text:

- Sharp dry pasta punctures thin bags and vacuum seals over time — pad the

  seal, the food isn't automatically spoiled, but its long-term clock
  restarts.
- Sugar, salt, and honey need no oxygen absorber (absorbers turn sugar into
  a brick). Honey keeps essentially forever; hardened honey re-liquefies in
  warm water.

## Protein depth

Canned fish and meat, pressure-canned home stock, dry-cured and salted meat,
hard cheeses in wax, powdered eggs and milk, and shelf-stable fats: ghee and
tallow are outstanding preparedness fats — shelf-stable for years, high
smoke point, calorie-dense (~9 kcal/g). Learn pressure canning if you want
to store low-acid foods (meat, broth, vegetables) safely at home; a boiling
water bath is only safe for high-acid foods (jams, pickles, tomatoes with
added acid). Follow tested recipes exactly — improvised canning is the main
modern source of botulism.

## Cooking without the grid

Options by scenario, with fuel math:

- **Butane/propane camp stove:** the workhorse. A 220 g butane canister
  gives roughly 1.5-2 hours of moderate flame; a 9 kg propane cylinder
  (~18 L of liquid fuel) runs a two-burner camp stove for tens of hours.
  Ventilate — every flame indoors makes carbon monoxide.
- **Rocket stove:** burns twigs and scrap wood with high efficiency
  outdoors; boils 1 L on a handful of sticks.

  Ventilate — every flame indoors makes carbon monoxide.
- **Rocket stove:** burns twigs and scrap wood with high efficiency

- **Wood stove / fireplace:** heat + cooking if you have one; store dry,
  split wood under cover (softwood ~1 year seasoning, hardwood 1-2 years).
- **Solar cooker:** free fuel on sunny days; a reflective panel cooker
  reaches 120-180 °C — slow but silent and fuel-free.
- **Thermal cooking:** bring a pot to a boil, then seal it in a heavily
  insulated box or dedicated thermal cooker; residual heat finishes rice,
  beans, and stews with a fraction of the fuel. This single trick can halve
  fuel use.
- **Cast iron and stainless:** cookware that works over open flame; nonstick
  coatings fail over campfire heat.

## Eating well under stress

Store what you eat, eat what you store: appetite fatigue is real, especially
in children — familiar food, spices, and some comfort items (chocolate,
coffee, honey) matter for morale. Aim for ~8,400 kJ (2,000 kcal) per adult
per day baseline, more for heavy labor and cold. Salt is critical and
nearly free — store several kilograms. A hand-crank grain mill turns stored
wheat berries into flour; without one, wheat berries still cook as a
porridge. Sprouting jars turn stored lentils and seeds into fresh greens
with vitamin C in 3-5 days — one of the few renewable "fresh" foods in a
long grid-down scenario.

## Garden and foraging notes

A modest garden of calorie-dense, cold-hardy crops (potatoes, cabbage, kale,
root vegetables) plus preserved harvest extends any pantry — grow what suits
your climate.

## Garden and foraging notes

A modest garden of calorie-dense, cold-hardy crops (potatoes, cabbage, kale,
root vegetables) plus preserved harvest extends any pantry — grow what suits
your climate. Foraging: never eat any wild plant or mushroom you cannot
identify with 100% certainty from multiple features; learn from local
experts and start with unmistakable species in your region (e.g. bilberries,
crowberries, and angelica in the North Atlantic). Wild greens like dandelion
and nettle (cooked) are widespread, nutritious, and hard to confuse.

chunks.title: Grid-Down Communication and Information
chunks.text:
# Grid-Down Communication and Information

*Educational information. Transmitting on amateur (HAM) bands requires a
license in nearly all countries; licence-free bands have power limits.
Listening is legal almost everywhere.*

## The layered comms plan

When mobile networks and internet fail, information flows in layers:

1. **Receive-only baseline (everyone):** a battery/hand-crank/solar AM-FM
   radio with shortwave coverage. Official emergency broadcasts, foreign
   broadcasters on shortwave, and (with SSB capability) even amateur traffic.
   Cost is trivial; keep one in the kit and one in the Faraday bin.
2. **Family short-range:** licence-free handheld radios — PMR446 in Europe
   (0.5 W, ~1-5 km real-world terrain-dependent), FRS in North America.
   Agree on a channel + backup channel and check-in times in advance.
   Real-world range is line-of-sight: hilltops help enormously, forests and
   buildings eat signal.
3. **Regional (licensed):** an amateur radio licence unlocks VHF/UHF
   handhelds through local repeaters (tens of km) and HF rigs that reach
   across countries with no infrastructure at all. Repeaters may run on
   backup power; simplex works when they don't. The licence exam is
   modest and the community actively trains newcomers — this is the single
   biggest capability jump available in comms.
4. **Data meshes (the new layer):** LoRa mesh networks — Meshtastic devices
   and Reticulum (RNS)-based systems — pass short text messages device-to-
   device over kilometres on licence-free bands at milliwatt power, with no
   towers, no internet, and optional encryption. Nodes are cheap
   (ESP32+LoRa boards), run for days on small batteries, solar-repeat from
   rooftops and hills, and the mesh heals itself as nodes appear.

chunks.title: Grid-Down Communication and Information
chunks.text:
bands at milliwatt power, with no
   towers, no internet, and optional encryption. Nodes are cheap
   (ESP32+LoRa boards), run for days on small batteries, solar-repeat from
   rooftops and hills, and the mesh heals itself as nodes appear. Reticulum
   in particular is transport-agnostic: the same network stack runs over
   LoRa, packet radio, WiFi, or serial links — infrastructure that
   individuals, not carriers, own. (Qortal-Hub mobile ships with RNS
   support, so a phone can participate in such a mesh.)

## Local-first information

Assume no search engines: keep printed and offline copies of the knowledge
you'd need — maps of your region (paper + offline map app with downloaded
areas), manuals for your gear, first-aid references, this handbook itself
stored offline, contact lists on paper. A cheap USB stick with scanned
documents in the Faraday bin, plus printouts in a waterproof folder, covers
both digital and analog failure modes.

## Family communication plan

Agree in writing, before anything happens: where to meet if home is
unreachable (a primary and a backup rally point), an out-of-area contact
everyone reports to (long-distance links often work when local ones jam),
radio channels and check-in schedule ("every odd hour on the hour, channel
4, listen 5 minutes"), and who picks up which family member. Text messages
often pass when calls fail — send texts, keep them short, and put phones in
low-power mode immediately in a blackout.

## Powering and protecting comms

Radios and phones are the highest-value, lowest-consumption electronics you
own — a 20 Wh power bank recharges a handheld radio several times. Standard
batteries across devices (AA/AAA with adapters, or USB-C everything)
simplify logistics.

chunks.title: Grid-Down Power: Sizing, Solar, Batteries, and Protection
chunks.text:
# Grid-Down Power: Sizing, Solar, Batteries, and Protection

*Educational preparedness information. Mains-voltage wiring and generator
transfer connections must be done by a qualified electrician — backfeeding a
generator into house wiring can kill line workers.*

## Start with the math, not the gadget

Two numbers decide everything:

1. **Peak watts** — the biggest simultaneous load you must run. A phone
   charger is 10-20 W, LED lights 5-10 W each, a laptop 30-65 W, a router +
   modem 10-25 W, a CPAP 30-60 W, a fridge 100-200 W running but 600-1200 W
   at compressor start, a freezer similar, an induction plate 1,000-1,800 W,
   an electric kettle 2,000+ W.
2. **Watt-hours per day** — load watts × hours. A modern fridge uses roughly
   1-1.5 kWh/day (it cycles); comms + lights + phones maybe 0.3-0.5 kWh/day;
   a laptop workstation 0.5 kWh/day.

Match gear to the numbers: a 200-300 Wh power bank covers phones, lights,
and a router for a day; a ~1 kWh station adds laptop and CPAP for a couple
of days; a ~2 kWh station (now available under 18 kg) keeps a fridge cycling
for roughly a day per charge — which is why solar input matters more than
raw capacity for outages beyond 48 hours.

## Solar recharging

Panels are rated at ideal conditions; real-world planning: a 100 W portable
panel yields roughly 300-500 Wh on a decent day (much less in Nordic
winters — plan 5-10x more panel or alternative charging at high latitudes in
December). Rules: point panels within ~30° of the sun and re-aim every
couple of hours; even light shade on one corner can halve output; keep
panels cool and clean. A 400 W panel array + 2 kWh station is a realistic
"fridge + comms indefinitely" summer setup.

chunks.title: Grid-Down Power: Sizing, Solar, Batteries, and Protection
chunks.text:
oint panels within ~30° of the sun and re-aim every
couple of hours; even light shade on one corner can halve output; keep
panels cool and clean. A 400 W panel array + 2 kWh station is a realistic
"fridge + comms indefinitely" summer setup. For permanent installs, an MPPT
charge controller, LiFePO4 battery bank, and proper fusing are the modern
standard — LiFePO4 gives 3,000+ cycles vs ~500 for lead-acid and tolerates
partial charging.

## Generators

Fuel generators deliver high power but need fuel logistics: a typical 2 kW
inverter generator burns roughly 0.5-1 L of petrol per hour depending on
load. Petrol stores ~6-12 months (longer with stabilizer); diesel and
propane store for years — propane-capable dual-fuel generators pair well
with the same 9 kg cylinders as your stove. Run generators outdoors, 5+ m
from windows, exhaust pointed away: carbon monoxide from generators kills
people in every major blackout. Run the fridge and charge batteries in
generator "shifts" of 1-2 hours a few times daily instead of running it
continuously — this cuts fuel use by 70-80%.

## Protecting electronics

- **Surge protection:** a whole-home surge protector at the panel plus
  point-of-use surge strips for sensitive gear covers most spikes. Surge
  strips wear out silently — replace after major surge events.
- **UPS:** for routers, NAS, and computers, a line-interactive UPS with
  automatic voltage regulation (AVR) rides through sags, spikes, and short
  outages and gives you minutes to shut down cleanly.

- **UPS:** for routers, NAS, and computers, a line-interactive UPS with
  automatic voltage regulation (AVR) rides through sags, spikes, and short
  outages and gives you minutes to shut down cleanly. Size it: UPS runtime
  claims assume full load; at 50 W of network gear, even a small unit runs
  30-60 minutes.
- **EMP/severe solar storm (worst-case layer):** the cheap insurance
  discussed in the preparedness community is Faraday shielding for spare
  electronics — a fully enclosed metal container (galvanized bin, metal
  ammo can, or nested cardboard-lined foil wrapping) with no gaps, contents
  insulated from the metal. Store: spare radios, a basic phone, USB sticks
  with documents, charge controllers, LED lights, and cables. Whether or
  not one expects such an event, the cost is a bin and an afternoon.

## The unplugged baseline

Electricity-free fallbacks so power becomes optional for survival: wool
blankets and sleeping bags rated below your climate's worst temperatures,
headlamps + lithium primary batteries (10-20 year shelf life; alkalines
leak), candles and an oil lamp with stored fuel, a thermos (boil water
twice a day, hot drinks all day), hand-crank radio, paper maps, printed
contact lists and manuals, board games and books. The goal of a power plan
is to shrink the list of things that truly need power to: refrigeration,
communication, light, and medical devices.

chunks.title: Heat, Light, and Sanitation Without the Grid
chunks.text:
# Heat, Light, and Sanitation Without the Grid

*Educational preparedness information. Carbon monoxide and fire are the two
killers in blackout winters — every combustion warning here is serious.*

## Staying warm when heating fails

Heat the person, then a room, then (maybe) the house:

- **Person:** wool or synthetic base layers (never cotton against skin when
  cold — it holds moisture and chills you), insulated hat and socks indoors,
  a hot water bottle in the sleeping bag, warm drinks and fatty food. A
  quality sleeping bag rated to your climate's extremes is a heating system
  that never needs fuel.
- **One warm room:** pick the smallest room on the sheltered side, close all
  doors, hang blankets over doorways and windows (most heat leaves through
  glass), get everyone + candles/lamp in it. Body heat alone keeps a small
  sealed room several degrees above the rest of the house.
- **Safe heat sources:** a wood stove is the gold standard. Portable
  paraffin/kerosene heaters and catalytic propane heaters rated for indoor
  use need a cracked window for oxygen and a working carbon-monoxide alarm
  with fresh batteries. NEVER heat with a barbecue, camp stove, oven left
  open (gas), or generator indoors — these kill quietly every winter.
- **Protect the house:** if freezing is prolonged, drip taps or shut off and
  drain water lines to prevent burst pipes; pour a cup of salt water or
  antifreeze rated for plumbing into toilet bowls and traps.

Recognize hypothermia early: intense shivering, clumsy hands, slurred
speech, apathy — treat with dry insulation, warm sweet drinks if fully
conscious, skin-to-skin or heat packs to the torso (not extremities first),
and gentle handling.

## Light

speech, apathy — treat with dry insulation, warm sweet drinks if fully
conscious, skin-to-skin or heat packs to the torso (not extremities first),
and gentle handling.

## Light

Priority order: LED headlamps (hands-free, efficient — a good one runs
50-150 hours on low), LED lanterns for room light, then flame (candles, oil
lamps) as ambience-plus-backup with hard rules — stable holders, away from
curtains, never asleep or unattended, one fire extinguisher and a smoke
alarm per level. Lithium primary AA/AAA cells store 10-20 years without
leaking; alkalines leak and ruin devices in storage. Rechargeables + a small
solar panel make light self-sustaining. Glow sticks are child-safe night
lights with zero fire risk.

## Sanitation: the underrated lifesaver

Disease follows failed sanitation within days. If the toilet won't flush
because the power or water is out, you still have options:

- **If sewer lines are intact** (power out, pipes fine): flush manually by
  pouring 6-8 L of any non-potable water (rain, pool, ditch) directly into
  the bowl in one confident pour.
- **If sewage may back up or water is too precious:** the twin-bucket
  system — one bucket for urine (low hazard, dilute and dispose away from
  water sources), one lined with heavy bags for feces, covered after each
  use with sawdust, ash, dry soil, or shredded paper to control odor and
  flies. Seal, store away from living areas, dispose per authorities later
  or bury 20+ cm deep, 60+ m from any water.
- **Handwashing is non-negotiable:** set up a station — jug with tap or
  bottle with pierced cap, soap, towel — beside the toilet bucket and
  kitchen. Alcohol gel (60%+) backs it up.

## Washing and waste

Dish hygiene without running water: three-basin method — hot soapy wash,
hot rinse, sanitizing rinse (capful of bleach per few litres), air dry.
Body: a 2-3 L "bucket bath" or pressurized garden sprayer with warmed water
keeps a person genuinely clean. Laundry: soak-agitate-wring in buckets (a
clean toilet plunger makes an effective agitator); wool clothing needs
washing far less often than cotton. Burnable trash reduces volume; food
waste attracts animals — bury or seal it.

chunks.title: Hunting, Field Dressing, and Home Butchering
chunks.text:
# Hunting, Field Dressing, and Home Butchering

*Educational information for lawful hunting and food preparation. Hunting is
licensed and regulated everywhere — seasons, species, methods, weapon rules,
and tagging requirements vary by country and region; know and follow your
local law, take the required hunter-education course, and learn hands-on
from experienced mentors. Firearms safety rules are absolute. Ethical
hunting means clean kills, no waste, and respect for the animal.*

## Before the hunt

The skills that fill freezers are unglamorous: scouting (tracks, droppings,
trails, feeding sign, bedding areas), understanding wind (deer smell you
first — hunt into the wind), patience, and marksmanship practiced until a
clean vital-zone shot is routine at your real distances. The ethical
standard: broadside heart-lung shots; if not confident, don't shoot. After
the shot, wait before following (a pushed wounded animal runs far), then
track blood sign carefully.

## The kill kit

Carried on every hunt: a sharp fixed-blade knife plus a spare or sharpener
(you will dull one), nitrile gloves, strong cord or zip ties, game bags or
clean pillowcases, a small bone saw (optional but helpful for sternum and
pelvis), paper towels, a headlamp, licenses/tags, and in warm weather a
plan to cool meat fast (ice in a cooler at the vehicle).

## Field dressing (gutting) a deer-sized animal

Speed matters: body heat spoils meat, so dress the animal promptly —
within the hour, faster in warm weather. The sequence experienced hunters
teach:

1. Move it to a clean, dry spot; on its back, head uphill, rear legs
   spread. Gravity is your assistant.
2. Ring-cut around the anus, free it, and tie it off with cord to prevent
   leakage into the meat.
3.

chunks.title: Hunting, Field Dressing, and Home Butchering
chunks.text:
ce experienced hunters
teach:

1. Move it to a clean, dry spot; on its back, head uphill, rear legs
   spread. Gravity is your assistant.
2. Ring-cut around the anus, free it, and tie it off with cord to prevent
   leakage into the meat.
3. First cut: pinch skin below the sternum, nick it with the blade tip,
   then open the belly skin down to the pelvis with the blade facing UP
   (two fingers under the blade as a guard) — shallow, cutting skin and
   membrane only. Puncturing gut or bladder taints meat.
4. Cut the diaphragm (the sheet separating chest from abdomen) free along
   the ribs. Reach up the chest, cut the windpipe and esophagus as high as
   possible, and roll the whole organ mass out in one steady motion,
   cutting connective tissue where it resists. The tied-off anus pulls
   through last.
5. Drain the cavity, prop it open with a stick for airflow, and cool the
   carcass as fast as possible — this single factor determines meat
   quality more than anything else. Gutting removes roughly 20% of body
   weight before the carry out.

Common beginner mistakes: cutting too deep on the opening cut, waiting too
long in warm weather, no gloves, and forgetting legal tagging before
moving the animal. An alternative in rough country is the gutless method —
skinning one side at a time and removing backstraps, tenderloins, and
quarters without opening the abdomen — worth learning from video and a
mentor.

## Hanging, aging, and skinning

Aging tenderizes: natural enzymes break down collagen after rigor mortis
passes (~24 h). Hang the carcass (skinned or skin-on) at 0-6 °C — a cold
garage in the right season, or a spare fridge for quarters — for 2-7 days
(young animals shorter, old animals longer).

chunks.title: Hunting, Field Dressing, and Home Butchering
chunks.text:

passes (~24 h). Hang the carcass (skinned or skin-on) at 0-6 °C — a cold
garage in the right season, or a spare fridge for quarters — for 2-7 days
(young animals shorter, old animals longer). Above ~7 °C, bacteria beat
enzymes: skip aging, process immediately, and get meat cold. Skinning is
easiest while the carcass is fresh and hung: cut around leg joints, open
the inside of each leg, and pull the hide down like a sock, helping with
the knife at the membrane, keeping hair off meat. A professional's warning
worth repeating: clean out everything under the pelvic bone early — organs
left there are the first thing to spoil on a hanging carcass.

## Breaking down the carcass

With the carcass split or quartered, the map of a deer (and, scaled, most
four-legged animals):

- **Tenderloins** — two small muscles inside the cavity under the spine;
  remove them at gutting/day one (they dry out on a hanging carcass) —
  the most tender cut, quick hot cooking.
- **Backstraps (loins)** — the long muscles along the outside of the
  spine; fillet them off whole. Steaks and medallions; do not overcook.
- **Hindquarters (hams)** — follow the natural seams between muscles with
  fingers and blade tip to separate the large roasts (top round, bottom
  round, sirloin tip); these become roasts, steaks, jerky meat.
- **Front shoulders** — more connective tissue: slow-cook whole, or cube
  for stew, or grind.
- **Neck, flank, trim** — grind (with 10-20% added fat for burger; venison
  is very lean) or slow-braise; bones become stock.

- **Front shoulders** — more connective tissue: slow-cook whole, or cube
  for stew, or grind.
- **Neck, flank, trim** — grind (with 10-20% added fat for burger; venison
  is very lean) or slow-braise; bones become stock.

Work on clean surfaces with a sharp boning knife, trim away hair,
membrane (silverskin), and any blood-shot tissue, keep meat cold
throughout, and package tightly (butcher paper, vacuum bags, or heavy
freezer bags with air pressed out) labeled with cut and date. Frozen at
-18 °C, well-wrapped venison keeps a year or more.

## Meat safety essentials

Keep raw meat below 4 °C except during active work; never let it sit in
the 4-60 °C danger zone for hours. Cook ground wild meat through
(minced meat mixes surface bacteria everywhere); whole-muscle cuts are
safer rarer. Wild boar and bear carry trichinella — cook these thoroughly
(the traditional cure-only preparations are not safe for them). When
regulations offer carcass disease testing (e.g. CWD in cervid regions),
use it. Anything that smelled wrong at gutting, was found dead, or shows
abscesses/lesions: do not eat it.

## Small game, birds, and fish

To field dress and skin a rabbit or hare: case-skin (the hide peels off
like a glove), gut it, and inspect the
liver — spotted livers mean discard (tularemia risk; wear gloves handling
rabbits). Birds: pluck for roasting or skin for speed; remove crop and
innards; hang game birds cool for a day or two for flavor. Fish: bleed
immediately, keep cold, gut early (slit vent to gills, remove all organs
and the dark kidney line along the spine), scale or fillet — a flexible
knife along the backbone, over the ribs, skin off last. Fish spoil fastest
of all; eat, salt, smoke, or freeze the same day.

## Preserving meat without a freezer

chunks.text:

knife along the backbone, over the ribs, skin off last. Fish spoil fastest

## Preserving meat without a freezer

- **Jerky:** lean strips 5 mm thick, salted or brined (traditional) or
  marinated, dried at low heat with airflow until they bend and crack but
  don't snap. Modern-safe practice adds a heat step to 71 °C.
- **Salting/curing:** dry-cure with coarse salt (traditionally with
  nitrite curing salt for safety in larger cuts) drawing moisture out over
  days-weeks; the ancestral method behind hams and salt fish. Learn exact
  ratios from tested recipes — curing is chemistry, not vibes.
- **Smoking:** hot-smoking cooks and flavors (eat or refrigerate);
  cold-smoking preserves only in combination with proper curing.
- **Pressure canning:** cubed meat and stock, following tested times —
  shelf-stable for years and the most idiot-proof long-term method.
- **Rendering:** fat becomes shelf-stable tallow (and tallow balm);
  bones become stock, pressure-canned or reduced.

chunks.title: Medical Preparedness and Field First Aid
chunks.text:
# Medical Preparedness and Field First Aid

*Educational information only — NOT medical advice and not a substitute for
certified training or professional care. Take an in-person first-aid course;
skills practiced under supervision are what actually work in a crisis. In
any real emergency, contact emergency services (112 in Europe) if at all
possible.*

## Training beats gear

Priority order: a certified first-aid/CPR course, then a wilderness first
aid course if you spend time remote, then gear. An untrained person with a
full trauma kit is less capable than a trained one with a bandana.

## The home kit, by layer

**Boo-boo layer (used weekly):** adhesive bandages in sizes, blister
plasters, antiseptic solution (povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine), tweezers
(splinters, ticks), small scissors, tape, burn gel, saline pods for eye and
wound rinsing.

**Wound layer:** sterile gauze pads and rolls, elastic (compression)
bandages, non-adherent dressings, wound-closure strips, larger dressing
pads, nitrile gloves in quantity, irrigation syringe (clean water under
pressure is the best wound cleaner), triangular bandages (sling, tie,
padding).

**Trauma layer (train before you buy):** pressure bandage ("Israeli"
style), hemostatic gauze, commercial tourniquet (know current protocols —
applied high and tight for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure
cannot stop; note the time), chest seal, space blankets (hypothermia kills
trauma patients), headlamp, trauma shears.

chunks.title: Medical Preparedness and Field First Aid
chunks.text:
, commercial tourniquet (know current protocols —
applied high and tight for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure
cannot stop; note the time), chest seal, space blankets (hypothermia kills
trauma patients), headlamp, trauma shears.

**Comfort/illness layer:** oral rehydration salts (see below), electrolyte
tablets, thermometer, common over-the-counter medicines you already use —
pain/fever reducers, antihistamines, anti-diarrheal, antacids — stored per
label and rotated; personal prescription medicines with the largest buffer
your prescriber and law allow (discuss an emergency supply with your
doctor; running out of daily medication is the most likely medical crisis
in any prolonged disruption).

## Skills that carry the most weight

- **Severe bleeding, deep cuts, and wounds:** direct, hard pressure on the wound with anything at
  hand beats searching for perfect gear. Elevate, keep pressing, do not
  peek. Tourniquet only for limb bleeding that pressure cannot control.
- **Treating a cut or wound when no doctor or clinic is available:** clean early and thoroughly —
  irrigate with copious clean (drinkable) water, remove debris, dress,
  change dressings daily, watch for infection: spreading redness, heat,
  swelling, pus, red streaks, fever. Infection signs = seek professional
  care with urgency; this is where field medicine ends.
- **Burns:** cool with running cool (not ice) water for 20 minutes, then
  cover loosely with clean non-fluffy dressing. Large, deep, facial,
  genital, or circumferential burns are emergencies.
- **Diarrhea and vomiting (adult or child), off-grid with no doctor:** the
  killer is dehydration, and children dehydrate fastest.

chunks.title: Medical Preparedness and Field First Aid
chunks.text:
ly with clean non-fluffy dressing. Large, deep, facial,
  genital, or circumferential burns are emergencies.
- **Diarrhea and vomiting (adult or child), off-grid with no doctor:** the
  killer is dehydration, and children dehydrate fastest. WHO-style oral
  rehydration: 1 litre safe water + 6 level teaspoons sugar + 1/2 level
  teaspoon salt, sipped constantly; continue feeding children. Strict hand
  and water hygiene protects the rest of the household.
- **Sprains/strains:** rest, ice/cool, compression, elevation; buddy-tape
  fingers/toes; improvised splints pad the limb in the position found.
- **Hypothermia and heat illness:** covered in the cold-weather and water
  chapters — recognize early, act early.
- **Tick bites (check skin after every walk in forest, brush, or tall
  grass):** what to do about a tick bite: remove the tick promptly with fine tweezers gripping at the skin,
  steady straight pull, no twisting or burning; disinfect; note the date
  and watch for expanding rash or flu-like symptoms in following weeks —
  these warrant medical attention.

## Dental and eyes

A dental first-aid kit (temporary filling material, clove oil, dental wax)
turns a screaming toothache into a manageable wait. Spare prescription
glasses in the kit — an old prescription beats no vision; consider one pair
in the Faraday/document bin.

## Hygiene as medicine

In every historical grid-down event, hygiene-related illness dwarfed injury:
handwashing, safe water, safe food handling (cook thoroughly, keep raw and
cooked separate, no room-temperature leftovers beyond 2 hours), and
sanitation discipline are the highest-yield "medical" preparations that
exist.

chunks.title: Household Preparedness Basics
chunks.text:
# Household Preparedness Basics

*Educational preparedness information for emergencies. Follow local laws and
official guidance during real events.*

## Priorities in order

A useful ordering for any emergency: shelter and warmth, water, food, light
and power, communication, security, sanitation, and morale. Most household
emergencies are mundane — storms, blackouts, supply disruptions — so prepare
for boring problems first and exotic ones second.

## Water

Store a minimum of 4 litres per person per day; two weeks is a solid
household baseline. Rotate stored water yearly. Have at least two ways to
make questionable water safe: boiling (a rolling boil for 1 minute; 3 minutes
above ~2,000 m elevation), a quality filter, and unscented household bleach
as backup (about 2 drops per litre of clear water, wait 30 minutes).

## Food storage

Build depth in food you already eat: rice, oats, beans, lentils, pasta,
canned meat/fish/vegetables, salt, sugar, fats, coffee/tea. Store cool, dark,
and dry; first-in-first-out rotation. Dry goods sealed in Mylar bags with
oxygen absorbers inside buckets keep for years — note that sharp pasta can
puncture vacuum bags, so pad or double-bag it. A pressure canner extends
storage to meats and low-acid foods.

## Backup power

Size backup power by asking two questions: what is the peak wattage of the
devices you must run, and how many watt-hours per day do they consume? A
small power station covers phones, lights, a router, and a CPAP; a ~2 kWh
unit can keep a fridge cycling. A UPS (ideally line-interactive with
automatic voltage regulation) protects routers, computers, and NAS boxes
through short outages and dirty power. Fuel-based generators need
ventilation, fuel rotation, and carbon-monoxide awareness — never run one
indoors.

chunks.title: Household Preparedness Basics
chunks.text:
-interactive with
automatic voltage regulation) protects routers, computers, and NAS boxes
through short outages and dirty power. Fuel-based generators need
ventilation, fuel rotation, and carbon-monoxide awareness — never run one
indoors.

## Heat, light, cooking

Blackout basics: headlamps beat candles for safety, wool blankets and
sleeping bags concentrate warmth in one room, and a camp stove or propane
burner (used with ventilation) covers cooking. A standard 9 kg propane
cylinder holds roughly 18 litres of fuel — know how many you have and check
fill levels rather than assuming exchange tanks are full.

## Home security fundamentals

Fix the weak points before buying gadgets: solid doors with long screws in
strike plates and hinges, locked windows, trimmed shrubs that remove hiding
spots, exterior lighting, and lived-in cues when away. Cameras and alarms are
layers on top of hardened basics, not substitutes.

## Documents, cash, comms

Keep copies of key documents (ID, deeds, insurance, prescriptions) in a
waterproof folder and encrypted digital backup. Hold some cash in small
notes — card networks fail in blackouts. A battery/hand-crank radio covers
official broadcasts; agree on an out-of-area contact person with family in
case local networks jam.

## Severe weather awareness

Learn your region's specific hazards and the warning signs. For example,
tornado clues include a greenish sky, sudden calm after strong storms, large
hail, a persistent rotating wall cloud, and a continuous freight-train roar —
when in doubt, take shelter in the lowest interior room away from windows.

## The 72-hour bag (bug-out / go bag)

One per person, packed and by the door — for evacuation (fire, flood, gas
leak), not adventure.

chunks.title: Household Preparedness Basics
chunks.text:

when in doubt, take shelter in the lowest interior room away from windows.

## The 72-hour bag (bug-out / go bag)

One per person, packed and by the door — for evacuation (fire, flood, gas
leak), not adventure. Core contents: water (1-2 L carried + filter or
purifier bottle + chlorine dioxide tablets), calorie-dense no-cook food
(nuts, bars, tinned fish — ~8,000 kJ/day), full clothing change with wool
socks and rain shell, sturdy shoes stored with the bag, shelter (emergency
bivvy or blanket + compact tarp), fire (lighter + ferro rod + tinder),
knife or multitool, headlamp + spare lithium batteries, first-aid kit with
personal medication for a week, hygiene kit, powerbank + cables,
hand-crank/battery radio, cash in small notes, copies of documents in a
waterproof pouch, paper map with rally points marked, whistle, work gloves,
duct tape, heavy contractor bags (shelter, poncho, water carry — a dozen
uses), and comfort items for children. Total target under 10-12 kg — a bag
you can actually walk with. Review contents every 6 months (clothing sizes,
medication dates, batteries).

## Vehicle kit

Blanket or sleeping bag, water, snacks, first-aid kit, headlamp, jump pack
or cables, tow strap, basic tools, work gloves, reflective vest and warning
triangle, phone charger, paper map, seasonal additions (ice scraper,
traction aid, folding shovel in winter). Keep the tank above half — fuel
stations fail with the grid.

## Community, cash, and barter

Lone-wolf survival is a myth: know your neighbors before you need them —
skills nearby (medical, mechanical, electrical), who has generators or
wood stoves, who is vulnerable (elderly, disabled) and will need checking
on.

chunks.title: Household Preparedness Basics
chunks.text:
cash, and barter

Lone-wolf survival is a myth: know your neighbors before you need them —
skills nearby (medical, mechanical, electrical), who has generators or
wood stoves, who is vulnerable (elderly, disabled) and will need checking
on. Hold two to four weeks of expenses in cash at home in small
denominations — card terminals, ATMs, and online banking all ride on the
grid. Practical barter depth beyond your own needs: extra fuel canisters,
batteries, lighters, water treatment, soap, salt, coffee, and skills —
these trade better than gold in short crises. Guard operational security:
casual talk about your supplies invites problems; the best preparation
looks boring from the street.

## Practice runs

Preps that were never tested fail in creative ways. Run a "grid-down
weekend": main breaker off Friday evening, live on your systems until
Sunday. You will discover which lantern eats batteries, that someone's
medication is at half, and that the camp stove's regulator is missing — on
a weekend when it's funny rather than fatal. Cook from deep storage
occasionally; rotate and re-date as you go.

chunks.title: Water: Storage, Treatment, and Sourcing
chunks.text:
# Water: Storage, Treatment, and Sourcing

*Educational preparedness information. Water safety mistakes cause illness
fast — when in doubt, treat twice (filter + boil or filter + chemical).*

## How much you need

Plan 4 litres per person per day minimum: 2 for drinking, 2 for cooking and
basic hygiene. In heat, exertion, illness (fever, diarrhea), pregnancy, or
for large people, drinking needs alone can hit 4-6 litres. A family of four
needs ~112 litres for one week — most households store a tiny fraction of
this. Two weeks per person is a serious baseline; grid-down water utilities
can fail within hours to days when pumps lose power.

## Storage that keeps

- Food-grade containers only (HDPE #2): purpose-made 10-20 L stackable jugs,
  200 L drums with pump and bung wrench, or factory-sealed bottled water.
- Never reuse milk jugs (protein residue breeds bacteria and the plastic
  degrades). Old soda bottles washed with a bleach rinse are acceptable.
- Store cool and dark; sunlight grows algae in clear containers. Off concrete
  floors on wood slats (chemicals can leach through plastic from concrete).
- Tap water from a treated municipal supply stores as-is; rotate yearly. For
  well water, add 2 drops of unscented 5-6% bleach per litre when filling.
- Emergency last-minute capture: fill bathtubs (a tub liner like a WaterBOB
  holds ~350 L clean), sinks, pots, and washing machines the moment trouble
  is announced. Your hot-water tank holds 100-300 L of drinkable water (turn
  off power/gas to it, let it cool, drain from the bottom valve) and toilet
  *tanks* (not bowls) hold a few litres of tap water if no chemical pucks are
  used.

## Treatment methods, ranked by what they kill

chunks.title: Water: Storage, Treatment, and Sourcing
chunks.text:
00 L of drinkable water (turn
  off power/gas to it, let it cool, drain from the bottom valve) and toilet
  *tanks* (not bowls) hold a few litres of tap water if no chemical pucks are

## Treatment methods, ranked by what they kill

| Method | Bacteria | Protozoa (Giardia/Crypto) | Viruses | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rolling boil 1 min (3 min above 2,000 m) | yes | yes | yes | Gold standard; costs fuel |
| Hollow-fiber filter (0.1 micron, e.g. Sawyer-style) | yes | yes | NO | Fast, cheap per litre; protect from freezing |
| Purifier bottle (filter + ion/adsorption media) | yes | yes | yes | Cartridge lifespan limited |
| Unscented bleach 5-6%: 2 drops/L clear, 4 drops/L cloudy, wait 30-60 min | yes | partial (NOT Crypto) | yes | Bleach loses potency ~1 year after opening |
| Chlorine dioxide tablets | yes | yes (4 h wait for Crypto) | yes | Best chemical option; long shelf life |
| UV pen / SODIS (clear PET bottle, 6 h full sun) | yes | yes | yes | Clear water only; UV pens need batteries |

To purify cloudy, muddy, or dirty water from a river, lake, stream, or
puddle: pre-filter first through a tightly woven cloth, coffee filter,
or a Millbank bag (a canvas drip bag that removes sediment), or let it settle
and decant. Sediment shelters microbes from chemicals and clogs filters.

## Practical toolkit

A resilient household covers three layers: a gravity or squeeze hollow-fiber
filter for volume, chlorine dioxide tablets as compact backup, and the
knowledge + fuel to boil. Add a dedicated "dirty" and "clean" bucket pair to
avoid cross-contamination, and mark them permanently.

## Rain and wild sources

chunks.title: Water: Storage, Treatment, and Sourcing
chunks.text:
ollow-fiber
filter for volume, chlorine dioxide tablets as compact backup, and the
knowledge + fuel to boil. Add a dedicated "dirty" and "clean" bucket pair to
avoid cross-contamination, and mark them permanently.

## Rain and wild sources

Rain catchment: a clean tarp or metal roof section feeding a barrel yields
about 1 litre per square metre per millimetre of rain — a 20 m² roof in a
10 mm shower collects ~200 L. First-flush the initial runoff (it carries
roof grime and bird droppings) and still treat before drinking. Wild
sources: prefer moving water, collect from the surface (not stirred-up
bottom), upstream of trails, livestock, and settlements. Never drink
untreated surface water no matter how clear — Giardia is invisible. Salt
water and urine are never drinkable and dehydrate you further; distillation
is the only way to reclaim them.

## Winter and hot climates

Freezing destroys hollow-fiber filters (cracked fibers pass microbes with no
visible damage) — sleep with the filter in your jacket or switch to boiling
and chemicals in winter. Melt snow with starter liquid in the pot; ice yields
more water per volume than snow. In heat, ration sweat, not water: rest in
shade through midday, work at dawn and dusk, and drink what you have — people
have died of dehydration with water still in their canteens.
